teile.einleitung: In a hairdressing salon, hair is washed, cut, coloured and styled. Hairdressers work here, looking after their customers' appearance.
wichtigste: A hairdresser works in a hairdressing salon.
In the salon there are mirrors, chairs and washbasins.
Hair is washed, cut and styled there.
Important tools are scissors, a comb and a hairdryer.
Cleanliness and hygiene are very important in the salon.
The word Coiffeur comes from French.

abschnitte.text: A **hairdressing salon** has big **mirrors** and comfortable chairs that can be adjusted in height. At the **washbasin** the hair is washed while you lean your head back. Scissors, combs, brushes and clips lie ready on trolleys. At reception you check in or make an appointment.

First the hairdresser talks with the customer about what she would like. Then the hair is washed and cut with **scissors, a comb** or **hair clippers**. After that he dries it with the **hairdryer** and styles it. Many people also have their hair **coloured** or highlighted. Some salons also offer beard care for men.

In the salon you work close to people. That is why **cleanliness** is very important. Combs and tools are cleaned regularly, towels are changed and hair on the floor is swept away. When working with colours and care products, hairdressers often wear **gloves** to protect their skin.

The word **Coiffeur**, used in Switzerland, comes from the French “coiffer”, meaning to style hair. In Germany people tend to say Friseur. In Switzerland you learn the job in a three-year apprenticeship as a **hairdresser EFZ**. There is also a two-year apprenticeship with a Federal VET Certificate. Enjoying contact with people and having skilful hands are important.

gewusst: Many hairdressing salons are closed on Mondays because they work on Saturdays.
In the salon you usually work standing up, often all day.

teile.einleitung: Cooks make sure that delicious food is served every day in restaurants, hospitals, care homes and canteens. The job requires skill, speed and great care.
wichtigste: Cooks usually work in the kitchen of a restaurant, but also in hospitals, care homes and canteens.
They prepare vegetables, fry, cook, bake and arrange the plates nicely.
In Switzerland you learn the job in the three-year apprenticeship as a cook EFZ.
Cleanliness and hygiene are especially important in the kitchen.
In large kitchens a whole team works together, known as the kitchen brigade.
Cooks often work in the evening and at weekends, when the guests are eating.

abschnitte.text: A cook prepares food. In the morning, goods are delivered and checked. After that the **preparation** begins: washing and chopping vegetables, preparing meat and fish, starting sauces. When the guests order, everything has to happen quickly. Finally, the food is **arranged** on the plate so that it also looks nice.

Most cooks work in **restaurants** and hotels. But there are many other places too: in **hospitals** and old people's homes they cook meals that suit people's needs, for example low in salt or soft. In **canteens** at companies and schools, hundreds of portions are made every day. Some cooks also work on ships or for a catering service.

If you want to become a cook, you do the apprenticeship as a **cook EFZ**. It lasts three years. You work in the training company and attend vocational school alongside. There you learn, for example, which nutrients are in foods and how to store goods correctly. For young people who find learning harder, there is the two-year basic training as a **kitchen assistant EBA**.

In large kitchens each person has a fixed task. This team is called the **kitchen brigade**. It is led by the **head chef**. A saucier is in charge of sauces, a pâtissier of desserts. This system goes back to the French chef **Auguste Escoffier**. That is why many kitchen words have French names.

In the kitchen the rule is: cleanliness first. Cooks wash their hands often and wear clean clothes. Raw meat and salad are cut on separate boards so that no germs spread. Food must be properly chilled. Because there are hot cookers and sharp knives, you work with concentration and care.

gewusst: Many technical words in the kitchen come from French, for example menu, dessert or sauce.
Cooking is a job you can do almost anywhere in the world.

teile.einleitung: Not all young people find an apprenticeship or the right path straight after compulsory schooling. A bridge-year programme is an interim solution that leads from school to an apprenticeship or to further schooling.
wichtigste: A bridge-year programme is an interim solution between school and apprenticeship.
Well-known options are the 10th school year, the pre-apprenticeship and the motivation semester (SEMO).
A stay as an au pair can also be an interim solution.
The integration pre-apprenticeship (INVOL) prepares refugees and young people who arrived late for an apprenticeship.
The transition from compulsory school to upper secondary level is called transition point I.
During an interim solution you keep applying for an apprenticeship.

abschnitte.text: The move from compulsory school to an apprenticeship or upper secondary school is called **transition point I**. Later comes **transition point II**, the move from training into the job market. Anyone who does not yet have a solution at transition point I can attend a **bridge-year programme**. It gives time to keep looking for direction and to fill gaps. An interim solution is an opportunity, not a defeat.

The **10th school year** is a well-known interim solution and usually lasts one year. There you improve your school knowledge and keep looking for an apprenticeship. In a **pre-apprenticeship** you usually work three to four days a week at a company and go to school one to two days. That way you get to know everyday life in a job. Both options prepare you specifically for training.

The **motivation semester (SEMO)** is aimed at young people who have no follow-on solution. It combines work assignments, lessons and help with applications. SEMO is a **labour market measure**. That is why **unemployment insurance** pays a large part of the costs.

As an **au pair** you live with a host family, help with the housework and the children, and learn a language at the same time. Many young people from German-speaking Switzerland go to the French-speaking part (Romandie) or abroad for this. The **integration pre-apprenticeship (INVOL)** lasts one year and gives practical preparation for vocational education and training. It is intended for recognised refugees, provisionally admitted persons, people with protection status S and young people who arrived late in Switzerland.

abschnitte.titel: Making good use of the time
abschnitte.text: An interim solution only helps if you use it actively. That is why **looking for an apprenticeship** continues during the bridge-year programme. You can do taster placements, write applications and get advice from the **careers advice service**. If you keep at it, you improve your chances considerably.

gewusst: The terms transition point I and transition point II describe the two big transitions on the educational path.
The integration pre-apprenticeship is also open to people with protection status S.
The motivation semester is paid for largely by unemployment insurance.

teile.einleitung: Gardeners sow, plant, water and prune. Some design beautiful gardens, others raise young plants in greenhouses.
wichtigste: A gardener plants and looks after flowers, trees and shrubs.
She sows seeds and raises young plants.
She waters, feeds and prunes the plants.
Many gardeners work outdoors, others in the greenhouse.
The apprenticeship as a gardener EFZ lasts three years.

abschnitte.text: Many plants begin as a small **seed**. The gardener puts the seeds into damp soil. After a few days they germinate and tiny leaves appear. Later she moves the **young plants** into bigger pots or into the flower bed. She also grows some plants from **cuttings**, which are shoots that have been cut off.

Some gardeners plan and build **gardens**. They think about where trees, flower beds and paths will fit. They lay lawns, build stone walls and plant hedges. Afterwards they come back regularly to look after everything.

Plants need **water**, **light** and **nutrients**. The gardener waters, adds fertiliser and loosens the soil. She cuts back shrubs and trees so that they grow nicely. She can tell when a plant is ill or has pests, and knows what will help.

The apprenticeship as a **gardener EFZ** lasts three years. There are different specialisms, such as **landscape gardening** or **plant production**. If you would rather do a shorter training course, you can choose the two-year apprenticeship with a vocational certificate (**EBA**). A good eye for colours and shapes helps with design.

gewusst: In greenhouses you can grow flowers and vegetables even in winter.
Gardeners also bring more green to towns and cities, for example in parks and on green roofs.

teile.einleitung: Roofers make sure that rain and snow stay outside. They cover roofs with tiles or other materials and often work high up in the fresh air.
wichtigste: Roofers cover the roof with tiles.
This keeps the house dry.
They usually work outdoors and at height.
Safety, for example with scaffolding and fall protection, is very important.
In Switzerland the job is part of the apprenticeship as a building envelope specialist (Polybauer) EFZ.

abschnitte.text: A roof protects the house from **rain, snow, wind and sun**. So that no water gets in, the roofer lays the **tiles** so that they overlap. The water then runs down over the tiles into the **gutter**. Under the tiles there is often **insulation** and a waterproof membrane. The insulation keeps the warmth inside the house in winter.

**Clay tiles** are the most common. But there are also roofs made of **slate**, **fibre cement** or sheet metal. In some parts of Switzerland you can still see **wooden shingles** on roofs and walls. Flat roofs, on the other hand, are sealed with special sheets. More and more often roofers also fit **solar panels** on the roof.

Anyone who works on roofs must have a head for heights. **Scaffolding** and a **safety harness** protect against falling. Good footwear and a helmet are part of it. Nobody works on the roof in storms, ice or thunderstorms.

In Switzerland you learn the job as a **building envelope specialist (Polybauerin or Polybauer) EFZ** in the specialism **roofing**. The apprenticeship lasts three years. Other specialisms include, for example, waterproofing, façade construction or scaffolding. If you like working outdoors and with your hands, this is the right job for you.

gewusst: A clay roof tile can last for many decades.
With solar panels on the roof, a house can produce its own electricity.

teile.einleitung: Healthcare assistants (Fachfrau or Fachmann Gesundheit) care for and look after people who need help. They work in hospitals, in care homes for the elderly or in home care.
wichtigste: A healthcare assistant cares for and looks after people in hospital or in a care home.
She measures temperature and blood pressure, for example.
She helps with washing, dressing and eating.
The apprenticeship as a healthcare assistant EFZ lasts three years.
The abbreviation for the job is FaGe.
After the apprenticeship you can train further in nursing.

abschnitte.text: Healthcare assistants work in **hospitals**, in **care homes for the elderly**, in rehabilitation clinics or for **Spitex**. Spitex cares for people in their own homes. Everywhere, these professionals look after people who are ill, injured or old. They work closely with nurses and doctors.

A healthcare assistant measures **temperature, pulse and blood pressure** and writes the values down. She helps patients with **washing, dressing and eating**. She prepares medicines as prescribed and changes dressings. Making beds and getting materials ready are also part of the job.

People who are ill are sometimes frightened or in pain. That is why the job needs **empathy** and a willingness to listen. Healthcare assistants explain what they are doing and are patient. Because patients need care around the clock, people work **shifts**, including nights and weekends.

The apprenticeship as a **healthcare assistant EFZ** lasts three years. It is one of the most frequently chosen apprenticeships in Switzerland. If you prefer to learn in a more practical way, you can do the two-year apprenticeship as a **health and social care assistant EBA**. After the FaGe apprenticeship you can study nursing at a **professional education college** or a **university of applied sciences**. Nursing staff are urgently needed in Switzerland.

gewusst: FaGe is one of the most popular apprenticeships in Switzerland.
Spitex makes it possible for many older people to live at home for longer.

teile.einleitung: Copyright protects works that people have created, for example books, songs, films, photos, drawings and computer programs. The person who created a work, the author or creator, may decide whether and how it is used. On the internet in particular, where everything can easily be copied, this right is especially important.
wichtigste: Copyright protects creative works such as texts, music, pictures and films.
In Switzerland a work is protected until 70 years after the death of its creator.
Computer programs are protected until 50 years after the death of their creator.
If you take a photo yourself, you own the copyright to it.
Uploading protected music without permission is forbidden.
With Creative Commons licences, creators allow use under certain conditions.
Works in the public domain are no longer protected and may be used freely.

abschnitte.text: **Copyright** protects works that a person has created with their own ideas. The protection arises automatically as soon as the work exists; you do not have to register it anywhere. The creator may decide who may copy, distribute or change their work. In Switzerland this is set out in the Copyright Act (URG).

In Switzerland a work such as a book or a song is protected until **70 years after the death** of its creator. For computer programs a shorter period of 50 years after death applies. After that a work enters the **public domain**, meaning everyone may use it freely. That is why today you may freely use, for example, fairy tales by the Brothers Grimm or music by Mozart.

In Switzerland you may use a lot of things for your own private use, for example listening to a song yourself. But it is forbidden to upload or publicly share protected music, films or pictures without permission. If you **quote** from someone else's text, you must give the source and mark the quotation as such. Special exceptions sometimes apply to schools, for example for copies used in lessons.

You are a creator too when you take a photo, paint a picture or write a story. Nobody may publish your works without your permission. But if a person can be seen in your photo, you must also respect their **right to their own image**. So copyright and personal rights apply side by side.

The organisation **Creative Commons** was founded in the USA in 2001 and offers simple licences. With them, creators can allow others to use their work under certain conditions. The abbreviation “BY” means that the creator's name must be given, “NC” means non-commercial and “SA” means share alike, passing it on under the same conditions. Many pictures on Wikipedia are available under such licences.

begriffe.erklaerung: The person who created a work.
An original creation of the mind, for example a song, a text or a picture.
No longer protected; everyone may use it freely.
Permission to use a work under certain conditions.
A passage taken word for word from someone else's text, with the source given.

gewusst: The © sign is not needed in Switzerland; a work is protected even without it.
In Switzerland the collecting society SUISA collects money for musicians when their songs are played in public.
A mere idea is not protected, only its concrete form as a work.

teile.einleitung: On a building site, new houses, roads or bridges are built. Many different tradespeople work together there, for example bricklayers.
wichtigste: A **bricklayer** usually works on the building site.
New houses and other structures are built on the building site.
Many trades work together: bricklayers, crane operators, electricians, plumbers and many more.
A **crane** lifts heavy loads high into the air.
Strict **safety rules** apply on the building site.
A building site is dangerous for children and is therefore closed off.

abschnitte.titel: What happens on the building site
abschnitte.text: On a **building site** something new is built or something old is rebuilt. It can be a house, a school building, a road or a bridge. First a pit is often dug. Then come the **foundations**, the walls and the roof. Finally the inside is finished.

A **bricklayer** usually works on the building site. Bricklayers build walls out of bricks, pour concrete for walls and ceilings and put up formwork. In Switzerland you learn the job in a three-year apprenticeship as a **bricklayer EFZ**. Bricklayers work outdoors in all weathers and need strength and skill.

Many **tradespeople** work together on a building site. The crane operator lifts heavy loads high into the air. Electricians lay cables, and plumbers put in water pipes. Carpenters make the wooden roof structure. The **site manager** or the foreman plans who does what and when, so that everything fits together well.

A building site is dangerous. There are big machines, deep pits and things that can fall down. That is why construction workers wear a **helmet**, safety shoes and a high-visibility vest. The building site is closed off with a **fence**. Children may not go in, but you may watch from outside.

gewusst: A big construction crane can lift loads of several tonnes.
Many cranes are operated from a small cab high up, but some are controlled by remote control from the ground.

teile.einleitung: An employer's reference is a letter from the employer that describes what work someone has done and how good their performance and behaviour were. You can ask your employer for one; in Switzerland, at any time. When looking for a new job or apprenticeship, it is one of the most important documents in an application.
wichtigste: An employer's reference assesses the performance and behaviour of a working person.
In Switzerland you can ask your employer for one at any time.
The right to it is set out in the Code of Obligations in Article 330a.
A reference must be true and at the same time worded favourably.
Instead of a full reference you can also ask for just a confirmation of employment.
You get an interim reference while you are still employed, for example when your boss changes.
After their apprenticeship, apprentices receive an apprenticeship reference.

abschnitte.text: An **employer's reference** is a written assessment issued by the employer. It states the type and length of employment, the tasks and an assessment of **performance and behaviour**. It is written on company letterhead and signed by a responsible person. New employers read it to get an impression of an applicant.

In Switzerland the right to an employer's reference is set out in the **Code of Obligations** (OR), in Article 330a. Employees can ask for a reference at any time, not only at the end of their employment. If specifically requested, the employer only has to issue a **confirmation of employment**, which states the type and length of the work but gives no assessment. For apprentices, Article 346a OR applies, which provides for an apprenticeship reference at the end of the apprenticeship.

A reference must be **true** and must not leave out anything important. At the same time it should be worded **favourably**, so that it does not make the person's future unnecessarily difficult. That is why many references are written in a special reference language in which small words mean a lot. “Always to our fullest satisfaction”, for example, counts as a very good assessment.

You get a **final reference** when a job ends. You can ask for an **interim reference** while you are still employed, for example if your boss changes or you want to apply for another job within the company. After a vocational apprenticeship, the training company issues an apprenticeship reference. After a holiday job or work placement it is also worth asking for a confirmation.

Read your reference carefully and check that all the tasks and dates are correct. If something is wrong or unfair, you can ask for it to be corrected. Keep all your references carefully, ideally as originals and as digital copies. In an application you usually include the references from your most recent jobs and training.

begriffe.erklaerung: A written assessment of your work by the employer.
A letter that only confirms the type and length of the work.
A reference you receive while you are still employed.
A Swiss law that, among other things, governs employment contracts.

gewusst: In Switzerland the right to an employer's reference only expires after ten years.
An employer's reference must not contain hidden secret codes meant to harm a person.
Even after a taster day at a company you can get a short report from the business.

teile.einleitung: The training company is the firm where you do your apprenticeship. There you learn the job in real everyday working life, supported by a vocational trainer.
wichtigste: An apprentice learns most of their job in the training company.
A vocational trainer shows how the work is done.
Alongside this you attend vocational school on one or two days a week.
A company needs a permit from the canton to train apprentices.
Training companies come in all sizes, from a small hair salon to a large corporation.

abschnitte.text: In Switzerland you usually learn a job through an **apprenticeship**. You spend most of the time in the **training company**. There you work alongside others from the start, first with simple tasks and later more and more independently. This way you not only learn specialist knowledge, but also how to deal with customers, colleagues and managers.

The training company has a **vocational trainer**. This person is responsible for the apprentices. She explains the work, gives feedback and records in the **training report** how the apprentice is developing. To take on this role you attend a course for vocational trainers. When there are problems, she is the first person to turn to.

The apprenticeship in Switzerland is called **dual vocational training**, because it combines practice and school. There are even three places of learning: the **training company**, the **vocational school** and the **inter-company courses**, where apprentices from different firms practise the basics together. For a company to be allowed to train apprentices, it needs a **training permit** from the canton.

Before you apply, a **taster apprenticeship** is worthwhile. You work in the company for a few days and see whether the job and the team suit you. Training companies come in all sizes. In a small company you know everyone, in a large one there are often several apprentices and different departments.

gewusst: In Switzerland tens of thousands of companies train apprentices, many of them small firms.
Companies that train apprentices secure well-trained specialists for the future, because many stay with the company after the apprenticeship.

teile.einleitung: Someone doing an apprenticeship is called an apprentice (Lernende or Lernender). In the past people also said Lehrling. Apprentices have special rights and duties, which are set out in the Code of Obligations, the Vocational Training Act and the Labour Act.
wichtigste: Someone doing an apprenticeship is called an apprentice (Lernende or Lernender).
Apprentices must follow instructions and work carefully (Art. 345 OR).
Up to 18, special protection for young workers applies, for example for night work.
Apprentices keep a learning record, and the company writes a training report.
At the end of the apprenticeship the company issues an apprenticeship reference.
There is no legal minimum wage for apprentices, only recommendations from the industries.
In the EBA apprenticeship there is expert individual support if needed.

abschnitte.text: Under **Art. 345 OR**, apprentices must do everything they can to reach the goal of their apprenticeship. They follow the company's **instructions** and work **carefully**. This also includes being punctual and attending vocational school regularly. In the **learning record**, apprentices note down what they have learned. The vocational trainer checks it.

The training company regularly records, usually once a semester, in the **training report** how the apprentice is developing. This is discussed together. At the end of the apprenticeship, under **Art. 346a OR**, the company issues an **apprenticeship reference**. It describes the training and, on request, can also assess performance and behaviour.

The **Labour Act** gives young people special protection up to the end of their **18th year**. **Night work** and **Sunday work** are in principle forbidden for them. There are exceptions only for certain jobs, when they are needed for the training, for example in a bakery. Dangerous work is also restricted. In addition, apprentices up to 20 get at least five weeks of holiday a year.

Apprentices receive **wages** that rise with each year of the apprenticeship. How much they are is set out in the apprenticeship contract. There is no **legal minimum wage** for apprentices, but many professional associations give **wage recommendations**. Anyone who does unpaid youth work, for example as a camp leader, can take up to one week of **youth leave** every year until the age of 30 (Art. 329e OR).

Anyone who has difficulties gets help. In two-year basic training courses with **EBA**, the Vocational Training Act in **Art. 18 BBG** provides for **expert individual support** if needed. This person helps with learning and with personal questions. In the case of conflicts at the company, apprentices can turn to the **apprenticeship supervisors** at the cantonal vocational training office.

gewusst: The word “Lehrling” is hardly used any more today; officially people speak of Lernende (apprentices).
Many apprentices do the vocational Matura alongside their apprenticeship so that they can later study at a university of applied sciences.

teile.einleitung: A pharmacist works in a pharmacy. She hands out medicines and explains how to take them correctly.
wichtigste: The pharmacist hands out **medicines** and advises customers.
She explains how and when to take a medicine.
Some medicines are only available with a **prescription** from a doctor.
Pharmacists have studied **pharmacy** at a university.
People who have done an apprenticeship also work in the pharmacy.
For minor complaints you can first get advice at the pharmacy.

abschnitte.text: At the **pharmacy** you get medicines, for example for a cough, a headache or a fever. The pharmacist hands them out and **explains** how to take them correctly. For example, she says how many tablets you may take and whether to swallow them before or after eating. In this way she helps make sure medicines work and do no harm.

Some medicines you can simply buy. Others you can only get with a **prescription** written by a doctor. The pharmacist checks the prescription carefully. She also makes sure that different medicines go well together. Today many pharmacies in Switzerland can also give **vaccinations** or give advice on minor complaints.

Anyone who wants to become a pharmacist studies **pharmacy** at a university. In Switzerland you can do this, for example, in Basel, Bern, Geneva or at ETH Zurich. The course lasts several years. You learn a lot about chemistry, biology and how medicines work in the body. People with a **vocational apprenticeship** also work in the pharmacy, serving and advising customers.

gewusst: Many medicines originally came from plants, for example from the bark of the willow tree.
In many places in Switzerland there is an emergency pharmacy service, so that you can get medicines at night or on Sundays too.

teile.einleitung: Digital ethics asks what is right and fair when dealing with computers, data and artificial intelligence. It is about questions such as: may a machine make decisions about people? And who is responsible if an AI makes a mistake?
wichtigste: Digital ethics deals with acting rightly and fairly in the digital world.
An AI recruitment tool from Amazon rated applications from women lower.
The MIT experiment Moral Machine collected millions of judgements about self-driving cars.
Explainable AI is meant to show how an AI decision comes about.
Dual use means that technology can be used both for good and for harm.
Shoshana Zuboff coined the term surveillance capitalism.
Automation bias means that people trust machines too much.

abschnitte.text: **Ethics** is the part of philosophy that asks what good and right action is. Digital ethics applies this question to computers, the internet, data and artificial intelligence. It deals with fairness, privacy, responsibility and transparency. Experts from computer science, philosophy, law and politics work together on it.

In 2018 it became known that an AI recruitment tool from Amazon rated applications from women lower. The AI had learned from old applications in which mainly men had been hired. Such distortions are called **bias**. That is why people call for **explainable AI**, so that humans can understand how a decision was reached.

What should a self-driving car do if an accident can no longer be avoided? In 2016 MIT started the online experiment **Moral Machine** on this question. In it, millions of people from all over the world decided whom the car should protect when in doubt. The results showed that people from different countries sometimes judge differently.

Many free services collect data about their users and earn money from it. The US researcher Shoshana Zuboff calls this **surveillance capitalism**. Her book about it appeared in English in 2018 and became known worldwide. Digital ethics asks how much data collection is acceptable and how privacy can be protected.

Many technologies are **dual use**: facial recognition can find missing children, but can also be used to watch people. Another problem is automation bias. People often trust automatic systems too much, even when they are wrong. One example is when someone follows a satnav blindly and drives into a dead end.

Not everyone has equally good access to the internet, devices and digital knowledge. This inequality is called the **digital divide**. It exists between rich and poor countries, but also between young and old in Switzerland. Digital ethics asks how everyone can take part in the digital world.

begriffe.erklaerung: Thinking about what good and right action is.
A distortion that makes an AI treat certain groups unfairly.
A technology can be used for useful as well as harmful purposes.
Too much trust in automatic systems.

gewusst: Amazon stopped using the controversial recruitment tool after the problem was discovered.
The results of the Moral Machine, with around 40 million decisions, were published in the journal Nature in 2018.

teile.einleitung: Careers advice helps young people find suitable training. An important tool for this is the website berufsberatung.ch.
wichtigste: Careers advice supports young people in **choosing their training**.
But the young people make the decision themselves.
**berufsberatung.ch** is the official website of Swiss careers, study and career guidance.
It is run by the **SDBB** on behalf of the cantons.
In the apprenticeship directory **LENA** you can find vacant apprenticeships.
Choosing a job is a **process** with several steps.
An **interest test** shows which jobs might match your interests.

abschnitte.text: Careers advisers support young people in **choosing a job**. They help you find out what strengths and interests you have. They show what training there is and how to get there. But the young people make the **decision** themselves. In Switzerland, careers, study and career guidance is the responsibility of the **cantons**.

**berufsberatung.ch** is the official website of Swiss careers, study and career guidance. It is run by the **Swiss Service Centre for Vocational Education and Training** (SDBB) on behalf of the cantons. For each job there is a **description** with the tasks, requirements, training and further training, often with photos and films too. The website exists in German, French and Italian, as orientation.ch and orientamento.ch.

On berufsberatung.ch there is the **LENA apprenticeship directory**. Training companies publish their vacant apprenticeships there. You can search by **job** and **place**. That way you quickly find out which companies nearby are looking for apprentices. Taster apprenticeships are also often arranged through such services.

In an **interest test** you answer questions about activities you enjoy. For example: would I rather work with people, with machines or with numbers? Afterwards you get **suggestions** for suitable jobs. These suggestions are a starting point. You then look at them more closely and try them out on a taster placement.

abschnitte.titel: Choosing a job as a process
abschnitte.text: Choosing a job does not happen in a day. It is a **process** with several steps. First you get to know yourself, then you explore jobs. After that you go on **taster placements**, make a decision and apply. This usually takes more than a year, often from the 7th to the 9th school year.

gewusst: Several hundred jobs in vocational education and training are described on berufsberatung.ch.
Careers advice is not only for young people: adults can also get advice on further training or changing jobs.

teile.einleitung: Vocational education and training is the official name for the apprenticeship in Switzerland. After compulsory schooling most young people choose this path and learn a job directly in a company. At the same time they attend vocational school.
wichtigste: Vocational education and training is the apprenticeship after compulsory schooling.
Most young people in Switzerland choose this path.
You learn in three places: at the company, at vocational school and in inter-company courses.
An apprenticeship lasts two, three or four years.
At the end you receive an EFZ or an EBA.
There are around 250 different apprenticeship trades in Switzerland.
After the apprenticeship many further training options are open to you.

abschnitte.text: Vocational education and training is training for a job, which you usually start at about 15 or 16. In everyday speech it is simply called an **apprenticeship** (Lehre), and the young people are called apprentices. About two thirds of young people in Switzerland choose an apprenticeship after school. The rules for it are in the federal **Vocational and Professional Education and Training Act**.

Switzerland has a **dual system**: you learn in practice and at school at the same time. On three to four days a week you work at the training company, and on one to two days you attend vocational school. In addition there are inter-company courses in which the basics are practised. In this way theory and practice are combined from the very beginning.

A three- or four-year apprenticeship ends with the **Federal VET Diploma** (EFZ). A two-year apprenticeship leads to the Federal VET Certificate (EBA). The EBA is meant especially for young people who learn in a more practical way. Afterwards you can often add an EFZ in the same job.

There are around 250 apprenticeship trades in Switzerland, from automotive specialist to healthcare assistant to IT specialist. The most popular include commercial employee, healthcare assistant and retail specialist. The content of each apprenticeship is set out in a **training ordinance**. It also lays down what is examined at the end.

An apprenticeship is not the end of learning. During or after the apprenticeship you can do the **vocational baccalaureate** and then go to a university of applied sciences. Professional education colleges and professional examinations are also open to you. With the Passerelle bridging course it is even possible to study at a university.

begriffe.erklaerung: Young people who are doing an apprenticeship.
Training in two places at the same time: at the company and at school.
A school that apprentices attend one to two days a week.
An additional qualification that lets you go to a university of applied sciences.

gewusst: Many countries study the Swiss apprenticeship system because it is seen as very successful.
Many bosses of big Swiss companies also began their careers with an apprenticeship.

teile.einleitung: Mechanics in the garage make sure that cars and other vehicles run safely. They check, service and repair, from changing tyres to tracking down faults with the computer.
wichtigste: A mechanic checks and repairs vehicles in the garage.
The tasks include changing tyres, changing the oil and checking the brakes.
During a service the vehicle is checked over regularly.
Modern cars have a lot of electronics, so faults are often tracked down with a computer.
In Switzerland the apprenticeships are called, for example, automotive specialist EFZ or automotive mechatronics technician EFZ.
In Switzerland vehicles must regularly go for the official vehicle inspection.

abschnitte.text: In the **garage**, the mechanic looks after cars that need servicing or repairing. He **changes tyres**, for example from summer to winter tyres. He does the **oil change**, checks the brakes, lights and windscreen wipers and replaces broken parts. With a **car lift** he raises the car so that he can see underneath it properly.

Modern cars are full of **electronics**. Many functions are controlled by small computers. That is why the mechanic often connects a **diagnostic device**. It shows where a fault is. With **electric cars** there is no engine oil change, but you work on the battery and the high-voltage system instead. This needs special training, because high voltages are dangerous.

Today the job of “car mechanic” has a different name in Switzerland. The apprenticeship as an **automotive specialist EFZ** lasts three years. The apprenticeship as an **automotive mechatronics technician EFZ** lasts four years and goes deeper into electronics. The two-year basic training is called **automotive assistant EBA**. You can specialise in cars or commercial vehicles.

A well-serviced vehicle is a safe vehicle. During a **service**, the mechanic checks the car according to a fixed plan. In Switzerland vehicles must also regularly go for the canton's **vehicle inspection**, MFK for short. Many garages prepare cars for it. In this way mechanics help to make sure that fewer accidents happen on the road.

gewusst: In Switzerland many people also call a mechanic a “Garagist”, although that word really means the owner of a garage.
A car is made up of many thousands of individual parts.

teile.einleitung: Every day in a bakery, fresh bread, croissants and Zopf are made. For this you need good ingredients and lots of tools, from the dough scraper to the big oven.
wichtigste: For bread you mainly need flour, water, salt and yeast.
The yeast makes the dough rise.
A kneading machine mixes and kneads large amounts of dough.
The ingredients are weighed out precisely on the scales.
The bread is baked in the oven.
In Switzerland the job is called baker-pastry chef-confectioner EFZ.

abschnitte.text: A simple bread is made of **flour, water, salt and yeast**. **Yeast** is a tiny fungus. It forms little gas bubbles in the dough, which is why the dough rises and becomes light and airy. Salt adds flavour and makes the dough firmer. For Zopf, milk and butter are added as well.

In the bakehouse people work very precisely. All the ingredients are weighed out on the **scales** so that the recipe is right. The **kneading machine** kneads large amounts of dough. The **dough scraper** is used to get dough out of the bowl. Then the dough is divided into portions and shaped by hand into loaves, rolls or plaits.

A dough needs time to rise. For this there is often a **proving cabinet**, in which warmth and humidity are set precisely. That way the yeast can do its work well. Some doughs also rest for a long time somewhere cool, which gives more flavour.

Baking is done in big **ovens** with several decks. With a long **baker's peel** you push the loaves in and take them out again. Smaller baked goods lie on **baking trays**. Because everything should be fresh in the morning, work in the bakehouse often starts in the middle of the night. The job is called **baker-pastry chef-confectioner EFZ**, and the apprenticeship lasts three years.

gewusst: In Switzerland the Zopf is a typical Sunday bread.
Without yeast or sourdough a bread stays flat and dense.

teile.einleitung: Learning does not stop after school and apprenticeship. Adult education includes everything that helps adults learn new things, catch up on a qualification or train further in their job.
wichtigste: The science of how adults learn is called andragogy.
Malcolm Knowles made the term known in the USA.
The umbrella organisation for continuing education in Switzerland is the SVEB.
The Continuing Education Act has applied since 2017.
Basic skills include reading, writing, maths and digital media.
Adults can catch up on an apprenticeship qualification after five years of work experience.

abschnitte.text: The science of teaching and learning in adults is called **andragogy**. The term comes from the Greek word for man or human being. It distinguishes adult learning from **pedagogy** for children. The education researcher **Malcolm Knowles** made the term known in the USA from the end of the 1960s. He described how adults tend to learn in a self-directed way and with their own experience.

On **1 January 2017** the **Federal Act on Continuing Education and Training (WeBiG)** came into force. It sets out principles for continuing education. It also governs the promotion of adults' **basic skills**. These include reading, writing and speaking in a national language, **basic maths** and using digital media. The federal government and the cantons support people in acquiring them.

Adults without an apprenticeship can also gain a vocational qualification. For this, the Vocational Training Ordinance requires at least **five years of work experience**, part of it in the job they are aiming for. Then admission to the **qualification procedure** is possible. Another option is the **validation of prior learning**. Here you show with a portfolio what you have learned at work and in everyday life, and you make up for what is missing with supplementary training.

Continuing education is offered, for example, by adult education centres, Klubschulen, vocational schools and universities. The **Swiss Federation for Adult Learning (SVEB)** is the umbrella organisation. It works for quality and good conditions. Anyone who wants to lead courses for adults can gain the qualification of **adult educator with a federal certificate**. It is part of higher vocational education.

gewusst: The word andragogy is built in a similar way to pedagogy but refers to adults.
According to the law, using digital media also counts as a basic skill.

teile.einleitung: The CV is an important part of every application for an apprenticeship. It shows the company at a glance who you are, which schools you have attended and what interests you.
wichtigste: A CV includes personal details, education, taster apprenticeships, languages, hobbies and references.
For an apprenticeship one page is usually enough, two at most.
The usual form is the CV in table format.
A recent, friendly portrait photo looks professional.
Personal details include your name, address, phone number, email and date of birth.
You state your language skills with the language and the level.
The information must be correct and in a clear order of time.

abschnitte.text: A CV gives an **overview** of you and the path you have taken so far. First come your **personal details**: name, address, phone number, email and date of birth, often also your nationality. Then follow your **education**, **taster apprenticeships**, languages, computer skills and hobbies. At the end come **references**, which are people who can give information about you, for example your teacher.

abschnitte.titel: Clearly set out as a table
abschnitte.text: Today the **CV in table format** is usual. The information is arranged in columns and clear sections, often with the year on the left and the school or activity on the right. A **clear order of time** is important. Often the most recent stage is at the top. For school leavers, **one page** is usually enough, two at most. An easy-to-read font and enough spacing make it pleasant to read.

In Switzerland a CV usually includes a **photo**. It should be recent and show you looking friendly and well groomed. A simple **portrait** against a calm background is best. Selfies, holiday photos or party pictures are not suitable. The photo is often the first thing the company sees of you.

**Hobbies** say something about your personality. A team sport, for example, shows that you can work in a team, a musical instrument shows persistence, and a role in a youth group or club shows responsibility. For **languages**, you state which language you know and how well, for example native language, good knowledge or basic knowledge. This helps the company to judge you better.

All the information must be **honest**. Read your CV through several times and ask someone to check it for **mistakes**. Keep it up to date when a new taster apprenticeship is added. If you send the application by email, it is best to save the CV as a PDF. Together with the covering letter and school reports, it makes up the **application file**.

gewusst: The CV comes from the Latin “Curriculum Vitae”, which means “course of life”.
Many companies only skim a CV at first, which is why a clear structure is so important.

teile.einleitung: In data analysis, data is collected, sorted and evaluated in order to gain insights from it. Companies, researchers and authorities use it to spot patterns and make decisions. Apps and websites also constantly analyse what you click on and how long you stay.
wichtigste: Data analysis means collecting and evaluating data and drawing conclusions from it.
Big data is often described with the three Vs: Volume, Velocity and Variety.
A correlation does not automatically mean that one thing causes the other.
The median is the middle value of a sorted list and is hardly affected by outliers.
In an A/B test, two versions are shown at random to different groups and compared.
Metadata reveals, for example, who phoned whom, when and for how long.
Third-party cookies from outside providers track users across many websites.

abschnitte.text: In **data analysis**, numbers and information are prepared in such a way that you can learn something from them. A weather service, for example, evaluates measurements to forecast the weather. An online shop looks at which products are often bought together. In Switzerland the Federal Statistical Office in Neuchâtel collects data about the population, the economy and the environment. Good data analysis needs mathematics, statistics and critical thinking.

**Big data** means huge amounts of data that can hardly be handled with simple methods. Big data is often described with the three Vs: Volume for the amount, Velocity for the speed and Variety for the different kinds of data. Every day an unimaginable amount of data is created worldwide by mobile phones, websites, sensors and cameras. It is stored in large **data centres**. To evaluate it, you need powerful computers and often artificial intelligence.

The **average** and the **median** are two ways of finding a typical value. With screen times of 10, 20, 30, 40 and 200 minutes, the median is 30 minutes, the value in the middle. The average here is 60 minutes, because the one high value pulls it up. Another example is the **conversion rate**: if 50 out of 2000 visitors to an online shop buy something, it is 2.5 per cent. Such figures help you to compare data quickly.

When two things increase or decrease together, this is called a **correlation**. In a town, for example, ice cream sales and the number of cases of sunburn rise at the same time. But that does not mean that ice cream causes sunburn. The real cause is a third factor, namely sunny weather. Anyone analysing data must therefore always check whether there really is a link of **cause and effect**.

Many websites carry out **A/B tests**: two versions of a page are shown at random to different groups, and you compare which works better. Cookies store information in the browser, and third-party cookies from outside providers track users across many websites. Phone calls produce **metadata**, that is, who phoned whom, when and for how long. Even such metadata reveals a lot about a person’s life. That is why data protection is so important.

To protect people, data is often **anonymised** or **pseudonymised**. With anonymisation it is no longer possible to find out whose data it is. With pseudonymisation, the name is replaced by a number, for example. But with extra knowledge, such as a list of the numbers, the data can be linked to a person again. Pseudonymised data is therefore still considered personal data.

begriffe.erklaerung: Huge amounts of data that can only be evaluated with powerful computers.
The middle value when all values are put in order of size.
Two things change together, without one necessarily causing the other.
A comparison of two versions with groups divided at random.
Data about data, for example when and how long a call lasted.

gewusst: The three Vs of big data were described by the analyst Doug Laney in 2001; later more Vs were added, such as Veracity for trustworthiness.
Even the ancient Romans carried out censuses to plan taxes and soldiers.

teile.einleitung: The trowel is the most important tool of the bricklayer. With the bricklayer's trowel you spread the mortar so that the stones of a wall hold firmly together.
wichtigste: With the trowel the bricklayer spreads mortar between the stones.
The mortar holds the stones firmly together.
Mortar is made of sand, a binder such as cement or lime, and water.
There are different trowels for different jobs.
The apprenticeship as a bricklayer EFZ lasts three years.

abschnitte.text: First the bricklayer picks up some **mortar** with the **trowel**. Then he spreads it evenly on the bottom row of stones. He sets the next stone on top and taps it into place with the handle of the trowel. He scrapes off extra mortar with the edge. Row by row, the wall grows.

**Mortar** is a mixture of **sand**, a binder such as **cement** or **lime**, and **water**. When it is fresh it is soft and easy to spread. After a while it becomes as hard as stone. This holds the stones firmly together and keeps the wall stable.

The **bricklayer's trowel** has a pointed or rounded steel blade and a wooden handle. With the **pointing trowel** you fill narrow joints. With a **smoothing trowel** you smooth plaster. In German the same word, Kelle, is also used in the kitchen for a **ladle**, which you use to serve soup.

The apprenticeship as a **bricklayer EFZ** lasts three years. Bricklayers build walls, set up formwork for concrete walls and ceilings and work on building sites for houses, bridges and roads. A love of physical work outdoors, team spirit and precise work are important.

gewusst: The Romans already built with a lime mortar, and some of their walls are still standing today.
With a spirit level the bricklayer checks whether the wall is straight.

teile.einleitung: How long you may work and when you must take breaks is set out in Switzerland in the Employment Act. It protects employees' health.
wichtigste: For office staff and industrial companies the maximum working time is **45 hours** a week; for everyone else it is 50 hours.
**Night work** is work between 11 pm and 6 am.
Anyone who works more than 7 hours is entitled to at least a **half-hour break**.
The daily **rest period** is at least 11 hours in a row.
For temporary **Sunday work** there is a 50 per cent pay supplement.
**1 August** is treated as a Sunday throughout Switzerland.
Employers must **record working hours**.

abschnitte.text: The **Employment Act** (ArG) sets out the maximum amount you may work. Under Art. 9 ArG, a limit of **45 hours** a week applies to industrial companies, office staff, technical employees and sales staff in large businesses. For all other employees it is **50 hours**. **Extra time** beyond this is only allowed in exceptional cases, usually no more than two hours a day. With a maximum working time of 45 hours, no more than 170 hours of extra time are allowed per year.

People who work need to recover. Art. 15 ArG requires a **quarter of an hour** break for more than 5.5 hours of work, a **half hour** for more than 7 hours and **an hour** for more than 9 hours. Between two working days adults must have at least **11 hours** off in a row. Under certain conditions this rest period may be shortened to 8 hours once a week.

Day and evening work runs from 6 am to 11 pm. Work between **11 pm and 6 am** is **night work** and in principle needs a permit. For temporary night work there is a 25 per cent pay supplement, and for temporary **Sunday work** 50 per cent. Some jobs cannot be done without night work. In **hospital**, for example, patients need help at night too, so nurses work in **shifts**.

According to the Federal Constitution, **Swiss National Day on 1 August** is a paid public holiday with no work throughout Switzerland. Other public holidays are set by the **cantons**. They can treat no more than eight of them as Sundays. That is why, for example, Corpus Christi or Berchtold's Day are not holidays everywhere.

So that it can be checked whether the rules are being kept, employers must keep **records**. Under Art. 73 of Ordinance 1 to the Employment Act, these include the hours worked, including breaks. Simplified recording is allowed for certain groups. Under strict conditions it can be dropped altogether. Checking is the job of the cantonal **labour inspectorates**.

gewusst: Stricter rules apply to young people: they may work no more than 9 hours a day and are entitled to a 12-hour rest period.
The Employment Act does not apply to everyone: agriculture and private households have their own rules.

teile.einleitung: The specialised upper secondary school (Fachmittelschule, FMS) is a school at upper secondary level. It prepares students for jobs in areas such as health, social work or education and leads on to professional education colleges and universities of applied sciences.
wichtigste: The specialised upper secondary school lasts three years.
The qualification is called the specialised school certificate.
After that you can do the specialised baccalaureate in about a year.
The specialised baccalaureate in education leads to a university of teacher education.
Typical fields are health, social work and education.
In 2004 the FMS replaced the former diploma school.

abschnitte.text: The **specialised upper secondary school (FMS)** belongs to **upper secondary level**, like the Gymnasium and the apprenticeship. It lasts **three years**. As well as general education such as languages and maths, there are subjects that prepare you for an **occupational field**. In **2004** the FMS replaced the former **diploma school (DMS)**.

Typical fields are **health, social work, education, communication, design and music**. Which ones are offered depends on the canton and the school. In all cantons a **work placement** in the chosen field is part of the training. That way you get to know everyday working life early on.

After three years you receive the **specialised school certificate**, often called the FMS diploma. With it you can go to a **professional education college**, for example in nursing. In about one more year you can gain the **specialised baccalaureate**, with lessons and a work placement. It opens the way to a **university of applied sciences** in the matching field.

Anyone who wants to become a teacher can do the **specialised baccalaureate in education**. It leads directly to a **university of teacher education**. There you can study, for example, to become a **primary school teacher**. This makes the FMS, alongside the Gymnasium, an important route into teaching.

gewusst: Before 2004 the specialised upper secondary school was called the diploma school.
A work placement is compulsory at the FMS in all cantons.

teile.einleitung: Painters paint walls, ceilings, building fronts, windows and doors. With paint they make houses more beautiful and at the same time protect them from weather and wear.
wichtigste: A painter paints walls, ceilings, building fronts, windows and doors.
Paint makes a house look good and protects it from damp and wear.
Before painting, the surface is cleaned, repaired and covered.
Painters work with brushes, paint rollers and spray guns.
In Switzerland the apprenticeship as a painter EFZ lasts three years.
A good eye for colours is important.

abschnitte.text: Painters work on new buildings and on renovations. They paint **inside walls** and **ceilings**, but also **building fronts**, windows, doors and railings. Paint has two jobs: it makes things look good and it **protects** them. A painted building front keeps out rain better, and a varnished wooden window rots less quickly.

Before painting, a lot of **preparation** is needed. Floors and furniture are **covered** with plastic sheeting, and edges are masked with tape. The painter fills holes and cracks with **filler** and sands them smooth. Often a **primer** goes on first so that the paint sticks well. Only then do the coats of paint follow, usually two.

The tools include **brushes** in many sizes, the **paint roller** for large surfaces and the **spray gun**. Painters know different paints and varnishes and know which is right for what. They **mix shades of colour** to the customer's wishes. Some also create patterns, lettering or special surfaces. For building fronts they work on **scaffolding**.

In Switzerland the apprenticeship is called **painter EFZ** and lasts three years. If you would rather do a shorter training course, you can choose the two-year basic training as a **painting assistant EBA**. You need skill, patience and a good eye for colours. Because you often stand on ladders and scaffolding, you should have a head for heights.

gewusst: White is the most common colour for inside walls, because it makes rooms look brighter and bigger.
In the past, painters made their paints themselves, for example from ground earth, lime and oil.

teile.einleitung: If you hand in your notice or are given notice, you cannot simply leave the next day. The notice period sets how long the employment continues after notice has been given. In Switzerland the Code of Obligations (OR) contains the most important rules.
wichtigste: After the probationary period, Art. 335c OR sets a period of one month in the first year of service.
From the second to the ninth year of service the period is two months, from the tenth year of service three months.
The period always ends at the end of a month.
Notice only takes effect when it reaches the recipient.
The periods must be the same length for employers and employees.
In case of illness there are protection periods during which the employer may not give notice.
Dismissal without notice requires a serious reason.

abschnitte.text: The **OR** sets periods that apply if the contract says nothing different. During the **probationary period** you can give notice with seven days. After that, **Art. 335c OR** applies: one month in the first year of service, two months in the second to ninth year of service, and three months from the tenth year of service. The period always runs until the **end of a month**. Different arrangements are possible, but must be agreed in writing.

Someone is in their third year of service and gives notice on **15 March**. The period is two months. Two full months are over on 15 May. Because the period has to run to the end of a month, the employment only ends on **31 May**. The day of delivery is also important: notice is a **declaration that must be received**. It only takes effect when it reaches the recipient, not on the day the letter was taken to the post office.

Under **Art. 335a OR**, the notice periods for employers and employees must be **the same length**. If the contract says something different, the longer period applies to both sides. This is so that neither side is put at a disadvantage. Anyone giving notice should ideally do so **in writing**, so that they can later prove when the notice arrived.

At certain times the employer may not give notice. These **protection periods** are set out in **Art. 336c OR**. In the case of illness or accident that is not your fault, they last 30 days in the first year of service, 90 days in the second to fifth year and 180 days from the sixth year. Notice given for unfair reasons is called **abusive**. It is still valid, but the court can award compensation of at most **six months' wages**. To get this, you must lodge a written objection before the end of the notice period.

Sometimes it is no longer reasonable to keep working together. In that case **Art. 337 OR** allows **dismissal without notice** for a **serious reason**. The employment ends immediately. A serious reason exists when, in good faith, the work relationship cannot reasonably continue, for example after a theft at the company. Courts examine such cases strictly.

gewusst: After the probationary period, an apprenticeship contract cannot be terminated with ordinary notice, but can only be ended without notice for serious reasons.
During the notice period you normally have to keep working and continue to receive your wages.

teile.einleitung: The right to your own image means that, in principle, you may decide for yourself whether photos or videos of you are published. Nobody may simply film you secretly and put the video on the internet. This right is especially important at a time when almost everyone has a mobile phone with a camera.
wichtigste: In principle, every person may decide for themselves whether pictures of them are published.
In Switzerland the right to your own image is part of personality protection in the Civil Code.
Anyone who wants to post a video of you needs your permission.
Before posting a group photo, you ask everyone in it.
If a photo has been published without permission, you can demand that it be deleted.
For children under 14, the parents usually have to agree as well.
As a background figure in a large crowd, consent is usually not needed.

abschnitte.text: The **right to your own image** protects your appearance, that is, photos, videos and drawings in which you can be recognised. In principle you may decide for yourself whether such pictures are published. Publishing means, for example, posting, sharing in a group or printing in a newspaper. Even secretly taking photos in private places can be forbidden.

In Switzerland there is no separate law just for pictures. The right to your own image is part of **personality protection**, which is laid down in Article 28 of the Civil Code (ZGB). There are also the Data Protection Act and the Criminal Code, which punishes, for example, secret recordings in private areas. Anyone who breaks this right can be required to delete the picture and sometimes to pay compensation.

Before you put a group photo of your class online, you ask everyone in it for their **consent**. For children under 14, the parents usually have to agree too. Secretly filming someone at the swimming pool, in the changing room or in the toilet and sharing the video is strictly forbidden. Such videos seriously violate a person’s personality and can even be a criminal offence.

Anyone who can only be seen as a **background figure** in a large crowd, for example at a football match or at a parade, usually does not have to be asked. People in public life, such as members of the Federal Council, may also be photographed at public appearances. But their private life is still protected. What always matters is whether a person is the centre of attention and can be recognised.

If a photo of you has been posted without permission, you can demand that it be **deleted**. It is best to take a screenshot first as evidence. Almost all social networks have a function for reporting posts. Get help from your parents, a teacher or from Pro Juventute on the number 147.

begriffe.erklaerung: The right to decide yourself whether pictures of you are published.
The permission that a person gives.
Legal protection for a person’s honour, privacy and appearance.
An important Swiss law about living together, abbreviated ZGB.
A person who can only be seen by chance at the edge of a picture.

gewusst: The Swiss Civil Code came into force in 1912 and still applies today in revised form.
Even a painted caricature can affect the right to your own image if the person can be recognised.
Many schools ask parents for written permission for class photos at the start of the school year.

teile.einleitung: ETH Zurich is one of the best-known universities in the world. It was founded by the young federal state and still belongs to the federal government today. Albert Einstein, among others, studied here.
wichtigste: When it was founded, ETH Zurich was called the Federal Polytechnic.
Teaching began in 1855.
It has had its current name since 1911.
The main building was designed by Gottfried Semper.
The second big site is on the Hönggerberg.
ETH is run by the federal government, not by a canton.

abschnitte.text: The law founding it was passed in **1854**, and teaching began in October **1855**. At that time the school was called the **Federal Polytechnic**. It was the first university of the young federal state, which had been founded in 1848. Since **1911** it has been called the Swiss Federal Institute of Technology. The abbreviation **ETH** is known all over the world today.

The main building stands above Zurich's old town. It was designed by the architect **Gottfried Semper**, who was himself a professor at the Polytechnic. It was built between **1858 and 1864**. Later **Gustav Gull** greatly remodelled and extended the building. From the terrace in front of the main building there is a wide view over the city.

As well as the centre, ETH has a second big site on the **Hönggerberg**. Among other things, the departments of **architecture, physics, chemistry and biology** are there. Since the beginning of the 21st century the campus has been expanded under the name **Science City**. There are lecture halls, laboratories and also flats for students.

ETH Zurich belongs to the **federal government**, which is why it is called “federal” (eidgenössisch). Together with EPFL in Lausanne, there are two Swiss Federal Institutes of Technology. Switzerland's ten **universities**, by contrast, are run by the **cantons**. ETH is particularly known for technology, natural sciences, mathematics and architecture.

**Albert Einstein** studied at the Polytechnic from 1896 to 1900 and gained his diploma there. From 1912 to 1914 he taught as a professor at the university. Later he received the **Nobel Prize in Physics**. According to ETH, more than 20 Nobel Prize winners are connected with the university because they studied, did research or taught there.

gewusst: Albert Einstein was first a student and later a professor at ETH Zurich.
More than 20 Nobel Prize winners have a connection with ETH.
ETH was the first university of the Swiss federal state.

teile.einleitung: Encryption turns a readable message into an apparently meaningless jumble of characters that only someone with the right key can read. The ancient Romans already encrypted messages, and today encryption protects billions of chats, payments and passwords every second. The science of it is called cryptography.
wichtigste: Encryption makes messages unreadable for unauthorised people.
In the Caesar cipher with a shift of 3, “HALLO” becomes “KDOOR”.
In symmetric encryption both sides use the same key; a well-known method is AES.
In asymmetric encryption you encrypt with the recipient's public key.
The security of RSA rests on the fact that large numbers are very hard to break down into prime factors.
With end-to-end encryption only the sender and the recipient can read a message.
HTTPS connections are encrypted with the TLS protocol.

abschnitte.text: The Roman general Julius Caesar is said to have encrypted letters by moving each letter three places along the alphabet. In this way “HALLO” (hello) becomes “KDOOR”, and anyone who knows the method simply moves the letters back. But this **Caesar cipher** is easy to crack, because there are only 25 possible shifts. In the Second World War the German Wehrmacht used the cipher machine **Enigma**, whose code was cracked by British experts around Alan Turing.

In **symmetric encryption** the sender and the recipient use the same secret key to encrypt and decrypt. This is fast, but both have to exchange the key safely somehow beforehand. The most important method today is called **AES** and was declared the standard in 2001 by the US standards institute NIST. It was developed by the Belgian researchers Joan Daemen and Vincent Rijmen.

In 1976 Whitfield Diffie and Martin Hellman published a method with which two people can agree on a shared key over an insecure channel. **Asymmetric encryption** builds on this: each person has a public key and a private key. You encrypt a message with the recipient's public key, and only the recipient's private key can open it. The well-known **RSA method** from 1977 relies on the fact that it is extremely difficult to break down very large numbers into their prime factors.

Messengers such as Signal, WhatsApp or the Swiss Threema use **end-to-end encryption**, so that not even the provider can read the messages. When you surf, the TLS protocol makes sure that connections with HTTPS are encrypted, which you can recognise by the little padlock in the browser. Passwords are usually not stored directly but as a hash value, for example with SHA-256. From such a hash value it is practically impossible to work back to the input.

A password made of 8 lower-case letters has 26 to the power of 8, about 209 billion possibilities. A computer making 1 billion attempts per second tries them all in at most about 3.5 minutes. With 12 characters made up of upper- and lower-case letters, digits and special characters, on the other hand, it would take an unimaginable number of years. So every extra character multiplies the work for attackers; trying all possibilities like this is called a **brute-force attack**.

begriffe.erklaerung: The science of encrypting messages.
A secret piece of information used to encrypt or decrypt.
Only the sender and the recipient can read the message.
A calculation rule that turns data into a short fingerprint.
An attack in which all possibilities are simply tried out.

gewusst: For decades the Swiss company Crypto AG in Zug sold encryption devices to many countries.
Future quantum computers could crack RSA, which is why experts are already developing new methods today.
The scytale of the ancient Spartans was a rod around which a leather strap was wound to encrypt messages.

teile.einleitung: Young people need special protection at work. That is why the Labour Act (ArG) and the Ordinance on the Protection of Young Workers (ArGV 5) set out from what age, for how long and what kind of work young people may do.
wichtigste: Under the Labour Act you count as a young person until the end of your 18th year.
Regular employment is in principle only allowed from the age of 15.
From 13, light work is possible, at most 9 hours a week during school term.
Young people work at most 9 hours a day.
The daily rest period is at least 12 consecutive hours.
Lessons at vocational school count as working time.

abschnitte.titel: From what age can you work?
abschnitte.text: Under the Labour Act, **young people** are those up to the end of their 18th year. **Art. 30 ArG** in principle forbids employment under the age of 15. From 13, **light work** is allowed, for example running errands. During school term this is at most 3 hours a day and **9 hours a week**. More hours are possible during the holidays.

Under **Art. 31 ArG**, young people may work at most **9 hours a day**. This may not be longer than for the other employees in the company. Compulsory lessons at **vocational school** count as working time. So school days are included in the maximum working hours.

Young people up to 16 may work until **8 pm** at the latest, older young people until **10 pm** at the latest. Night and Sunday work is only allowed with a special permit. Between two working days, young people need at least **12 hours of rest** in one go. For adults it is eleven hours.

**Dangerous work** is in principle forbidden for young people. This includes, for example, work with dangerous machines or substances. There is an exception for apprentices aged 15 and over if the **training ordinance** for the job allows it. Then accompanying safety measures must be followed.

In the past children also worked in factories, often for many hours a day. The **Federal Factory Act of 1877** banned factory work for children under 14. It also introduced the **11-hour day**. The law is seen as a milestone in the protection of workers in Switzerland.

gewusst: Special rules apply to performances in culture, art and sport, so younger children may also take part under certain conditions.
The cantonal labour inspectorates make sure the Labour Act is followed.

teile.einleitung: Clickbait means sensational headlines or pictures on the internet whose main purpose is to make you click on them. The English word means a lure for clicks. Often the headline promises much more than the article or video then delivers.
wichtigste: Clickbait means sensational headlines or pictures that are only meant to tempt you to click.
The English word means something like “a lure for clicks” (Klickköder in German).
Clickbait works with curiosity, exaggeration and strong feelings.
Behind clickbait there is often the aim of making money with advertising.
Typical are sentences such as “You won’t believe what happened next”.
Clickbait can also lead to false news or dangerous websites.

abschnitte.text: **Clickbait** is made up of the English words “click” and “bait”. Like a worm on a fishing hook, a headline or preview picture is meant to lure people in. Usually something exciting is promised but not revealed. If you are curious, you click to find out. Often the content then turns out to be disappointing or quite different from what you expected.

Clickbait takes advantage of **curiosity**; people also speak of a curiosity gap. Typical headlines are “You won’t believe what happened next” or “Number 7 will shock you”. Words such as “unbelievable” or “shocking” and lots of exclamation marks are also common. With videos, preview pictures often show exaggerated faces, red arrows and circles. Sometimes a picture is shown that does not appear in the video at all.

Many websites and video channels earn money with **advertising**. The more people click, the more advertising is seen and the more money comes in. The algorithms of social networks also reward content with lots of clicks. That is why some people deliberately use clickbait. For serious journalism this is a problem, because exaggeration can destroy trust.

Clickbait is often just annoying, but it can also be dangerous. Some links lead to **false news** or to pages with malware. Others want to steal personal data or passwords; this is called **phishing**. So-called prize draws with “You have won a mobile phone!” are part of this too. The rule here is: do not click and do not enter any data.

A good tip is to ask yourself before clicking who is behind the **source** and what it wants to achieve. Serious media usually already state the most important point in the headline. Exaggerated promises, time pressure and lots of exclamation marks are warning signs. If you are unsure, look for the news in a well-known newspaper or on SRF. And sometimes the best thing is simply to keep scrolling.

begriffe.erklaerung: A sensational headline or picture meant to tempt you to click.
Something used to lure, for example a worm on a fishing hook.
Fraud in which someone on the internet tries to steal passwords or data.
A report that deliberately spreads false information.
Where a piece of information comes from, for example a newspaper or website.

gewusst: Long before the internet, tabloid newspapers sold more copies at the kiosk with sensational headlines.
In 2016 Facebook announced that it would show clickbait posts less often in the news feed.

teile.einleitung: Your digital identity is all the features by which you are recognised on the internet: username, profile picture, email address, passwords and much more. It is like an ID card for the online world. Because it is so valuable, you have to protect it well.
wichtigste: Your digital identity includes all the features by which you are recognised online.
A secure password is long and contains different kinds of characters.
You should use a separate password for each account.
A password manager stores many passwords securely encrypted.
In identity theft, someone uses another person’s data to pretend to be that person.
In September 2025 Swiss voters accepted the law on the state e-ID.

abschnitte.text: Your **digital identity** includes usernames, profile pictures, email addresses, posts and account details. You choose some parts yourself, for example a nickname or an **avatar**, a graphic figure that represents you online. Other parts come about automatically, for example through data that apps collect. Together they form the picture that others have of you online.

A secure **password** is long and contains capital and small letters, numbers and special characters. Passphrases made of several random words, which are easy to remember, are also good. Each account needs its own password, because otherwise all your accounts are at risk if there is a data leak. A **password manager** stores all your passwords encrypted, and you only have to remember one master password.

In **identity theft**, someone uses another person’s data to pretend to be them. The criminals, for example, order goods in someone else’s name or write messages in the victim’s name. They often get the data through phishing emails or stolen passwords. Two-factor authentication makes this much harder for them.

A **fake profile** is an account with a false identity. Some fake profiles use photos of real people who know nothing about it. They are used for fraud, bullying or to gain trust dishonestly. If you discover a fake profile with your own picture, you can report it to the platform.

The **e-ID** is a state electronic identity card for your mobile phone. A first law, under which private companies would have issued the e-ID, was rejected by voters in 2021. In September 2025 they narrowly accepted a new law under which the Confederation issues the e-ID itself.
