abschnitte.text: Many Swiss farms have **cows**. They are fed and milked every day, even on Sundays. There are also farms with **pigs, hens, sheep or goats**. The farmer makes sure the animals are healthy and have enough space. If an animal is ill, she calls the vet.

**Grain, potatoes, sugar beet or vegetables** grow in the fields. Sowing is done in spring, and harvesting in summer and autumn. Grass grows in the meadows and is dried as hay for the winter. For this, big **machines** such as tractors and combine harvesters are needed. Some farms also have fruit trees or vines.

Much of the land in Switzerland is hilly or lies in the mountains. There it is mainly suitable for meadows and pastures. In summer many animals move up to the **alpine pastures**. The **federal government** supports farming families with **direct payments**, for example for looking after the landscape and for animal-friendly farming. Many farms also sell their produce directly in a **farm shop**.

Anyone who wants to learn the job does a three-year apprenticeship as a **farmer EFZ**. After that there is further training, such as the **farm management school**. For women who run the household and the farm together, there is also further training as a **farmer's wife with a federal certificate**. There is a lot to do on a farm: animals, fields, machines and office work too.

gewusst: Cows have to be milked every day, even on public holidays.
In summer many Swiss cows spend a few weeks on the alpine pastures.

teile.einleitung: Bus drivers take lots of people to school, to work or home every day. They drive according to a timetable from stop to stop, in towns and in the countryside.
wichtigste: Bus drivers drive a bus with passengers according to a timetable.
They stop at the bus stops and take people to where they are going.
For a service bus you need a category D driving licence.
Safety and punctuality are particularly important.
In Switzerland buses run in towns and, as the PostBus, out to remote villages too.

abschnitte.text: A bus driver drives a fixed **route**. The **timetable** says when he must be at which stop. Before setting off, he checks that the bus is in order. On the way he watches out for traffic, bikes and people at the side of the road. He often works **shifts**, early in the morning, in the evening or at weekends.

Bus drivers help passengers with questions about connections. They wait until everyone has got on safely and then pull away gently. There is often a **ramp** for people in wheelchairs or with pushchairs. Being friendly and patient is part of the job. They stay calm even at hectic moments.

To drive a big bus with passengers you need a **category D driving licence**. In addition, Switzerland requires professional drivers to have a **certificate of professional competence**, for which they regularly attend further training. Many people only learn the job as adults, after first training for a different job. Transport companies often train new drivers themselves.

In towns buses often run at regular intervals. In the countryside and the mountains the yellow **PostBus** runs. It also connects small villages with the railway station. Some routes go over narrow mountain pass roads. There it takes a particularly high level of skill at the wheel.

gewusst: The PostBus can be recognised by its yellow paintwork and its three-note horn.
Many city buses now run on electricity instead of diesel.

teile.einleitung: With an application you show a company that you would like to do an apprenticeship with them. It includes a covering letter, a CV and your school reports. A careful application is your ticket to an interview.
wichtigste: An application consists of a covering letter, a CV and school reports.
Reports from taster placements and test results are often added.
The documents together are also called the application file.
Today you usually apply by email or through an online portal.
Spelling and care are very important.
A good application is often followed by an interview.

abschnitte.text: An **application file** contains a covering letter, a CV and copies of your school reports. Many companies also want to see reports from taster placements. Some ask for results from aptitude tests such as the **Multicheck** or the Basic-Check. Everything should be neat, complete and easy to read.

In the **covering letter** you explain why you want to learn exactly this job. You also write why you want to work at this particular company. Concrete examples are good, such as experiences from your taster placement. The letter should be no longer than one page.

The **CV** shows at a glance who you are. It includes your name, address, date of birth, the schools you have attended and the languages you know. Hobbies, clubs or small jobs such as babysitting also belong in it. In Switzerland it is still usual to add a friendly photo.

Today most companies want applications by email or through a form on their website. It is best to send the documents as a **PDF**. You can find vacant apprenticeships on berufsberatung.ch and on apprenticeship job boards. Many companies give out apprenticeships a year before they start.

If the company likes your application, you are invited to an **interview**. You should arrive on time, look tidy and be well prepared. It helps to find out about the company beforehand and to bring your own questions. You should not give up after rejections, because almost everyone gets several of them.

begriffe.erklaerung: All the documents of an application together.
A letter in which you explain why you want the position.
An overview of yourself, your schools and your experience.
An aptitude test that many training companies ask for.

gewusst: Many apprentices write ten or more applications before they find an apprenticeship.
A single typing mistake in the company's name can make a bad impression, so it is worth having it proofread.

teile.einleitung: Disinformation means false or misleading information that is spread deliberately in order to deceive people. There are often political or financial aims behind it. If you know the tricks, you are less likely to fall for it.
wichtigste: Disinformation is spread deliberately in order to deceive.
Misinformation, on the other hand, is false but is passed on without bad intentions.
Social bots are automatic accounts that behave like people.
The Internet Research Agency in St Petersburg became known as a Russian troll factory.
According to an MIT study from 2018, false reports spread faster on Twitter than true ones.
Lateral reading and prebunking help against disinformation.

abschnitte.text: **Disinformation** is a deliberate lie that looks like real information. By contrast, **misinformation** is a mistake: someone shares something false but believes it themselves. Disinformation can be completely made up or can take real facts out of context. It is often meant to trigger fear or anger, because such feelings make people share things.

Behind disinformation there are sometimes states that want to influence other countries. One well-known example is the **Internet Research Agency** in St Petersburg, a Russian troll factory in which employees stirred up feeling using fake accounts. Others spread lies to earn money from clicks and advertising. Automatic **social bots** also help to repeat false messages thousands of times.

Researchers at MIT studied millions of tweets and published their study in the journal Science in 2018. They found that false reports spread faster and further than true ones. One reason is that false stories often seem newer and more surprising. In addition, it was mainly people, not just bots, who spread the false reports further.

Our brain makes things easy for disinformation. With the **illusory truth effect**, a statement seems more believable if you have heard it often, even if it is false. With **confirmation bias**, we mainly believe information that matches our opinion. If you know about these effects, you can check things more consciously.

With **lateral reading**, you open other sources to find out who is behind an unknown website. Fact-checking sites and serious media help to check claims. With **prebunking**, you learn about typical tricks of deception in advance, similar to the way a vaccination prepares the body. And before you share something, it is worth pausing briefly to think.

begriffe.erklaerung: False information spread on purpose.
False information passed on without bad intentions.
An organisation in which people deliberately stir up feeling using fake accounts.
Learning about tricks of deception in advance, to protect yourself.

gewusst: According to the MIT study of 2018, false reports on Twitter were passed on much more often than true ones.
Disinformation is not new: even in ancient times, rulers deliberately spread rumours about their opponents.

teile.einleitung: On the building site, the workers wear a hard helmet. It protects their heads if something falls down or if they bump into something.
wichtigste: The **hard hat** protects the head from injury.
On a building site something can fall from above.
You can also bang your head on beams or scaffolding.
The helmet is made of hard **plastic** and padded inside.
A hard hat must fit well to protect you properly.
On many building sites wearing a helmet is compulsory.

abschnitte.text: On a **building site** people work high up, for example on scaffolding or with the crane. A tool, a stone or a piece of wood can fall down. The **hard hat** protects the head from such injuries. It also helps if you bang your head on a beam or a pipe.

A hard hat has a tough shell made of **plastic**. Inside there are straps that keep the helmet a little way away from the head. If something falls on the helmet, the blow is spread out and the head is hit less hard. With a small wheel or strap you can adjust the helmet to fit your head exactly. Only a helmet that fits well protects you properly.

As well as the helmet, construction workers often wear **safety shoes**, gloves and a bright **high-visibility vest**. On many building sites wearing a helmet is compulsory. In Switzerland **Suva** works to prevent accidents at work. Because plastic ages over time, a helmet has to be replaced after a few years.

gewusst: On many building sites visitors also have to wear a helmet.
A helmet that has taken a heavy blow should be replaced, even if you cannot see any damage.

teile.einleitung: The watering can is a simple but important tool in the garden. With it, plants get exactly as much water as they need.
wichtigste: You use a watering can to water plants in the garden, on the balcony and indoors.
It has a container, a handle and a long spout.
A rose can sit at the front of the spout to spread the water finely.
Without water, plants wilt.
Besides the watering can, gardeners often also need a hose.

abschnitte.text: A watering can consists of a **container** for the water, a **handle** and a long pipe. The pipe is called the **spout**. At the front you can fit a **rose**. It has lots of small holes so that the water comes out like fine rain. This way delicate little plants are not washed away.

Plants take up water from the soil with their **roots**. Nutrients also get into the plant with the water. Without water the leaves go limp and the plant **wilts**. But too much water is also harmful, because the roots can then rot.

It is best to water in the **morning** or the **evening**, when it is cooler. Then less water evaporates. You water directly onto the soil and not over the leaves. Collected **rainwater** is particularly good for many plants.

For **gardeners**, watering is part of everyday life. Nurseries and greenhouses often have automatic watering systems. But for single pots and young plants the watering can is still practical. Florists also use it in the flower shop.

gewusst: Many watering cans hold about ten litres of water. So when they are full they are quite heavy.
Rainwater contains less lime than tap water, which some plants particularly like.

teile.einleitung: A website is a presence on the internet made up of one or many individual web pages, for example the website of a zoo, a school or a newspaper. You open it with a browser by typing in its address or clicking on a link. The World Wide Web, on which all websites are found, was invented at CERN in Geneva in 1989.
wichtigste: A website consists of one or more web pages.
You look at web pages with a browser.
You type the address of a website into the address bar.
Many Swiss internet addresses end in .ch.
If you click on a link, another page opens.
A small padlock next to the address shows a protected connection.
The start page of a website is often called the homepage.

abschnitte.text: A **website** is a whole presence on the internet, while a **web page** is a single page of it. The start page, where you usually land first, is often called the **homepage**. From there, links lead to other pages, for example opening times, pictures or contact details. There are more than a billion websites worldwide, but many of them are hardly used.

To look at websites you need a **browser**, for example Chrome, Safari, Firefox or Edge. You type the address of a website, such as “www.sbb.ch”, into the address bar at the top. Clicking on a link opens another page; this is called surfing. A small padlock next to the address shows that the connection is encrypted with HTTPS and protected.

Every address finishes with an ending called the **top-level domain**. Many Swiss websites end in .ch, which comes from “Confoederatio Helvetica”. For some years there has also been the ending .swiss. Other well-known endings are .de for Germany, .com for companies and .org for organisations.

Web pages are written in the language **HTML**, which sets out where headings, texts, pictures and links go. CSS is used to decide colours and fonts, and JavaScript makes pages move and become interactive. The finished files are kept on a server, a computer that is connected to the internet day and night. Today you can also create your own website with website builders, without knowing how to program.

In 1989 the British physicist **Tim Berners-Lee** developed the World Wide Web at the CERN research centre in Geneva. He wanted to help researchers share information easily. In 1991 the world's first website went online; it explained what the web is. In 1993 CERN released the technology free of charge for everyone, which made the web possible worldwide.

begriffe.erklaerung: A program you use to look at web pages.
A clickable reference that takes you to another page.
The start page of a website.
The language in which web pages are written.
The name of a website, for example sbb.ch.

gewusst: The world's first website ran on a computer at CERN and can still be viewed today as a reconstruction.
The abbreviation www stands for World Wide Web.
If a page frightens you, simply close it and tell an adult.

teile.einleitung: An apprenticeship place is a training position in a company where you can do an apprenticeship. The search for one usually begins in the second-to-last year of school and takes time, planning and persistence.
wichtigste: You find vacant apprenticeship places mainly on online apprenticeship exchanges such as LENA, on company websites and through contacts.
You send a speculative application to a company that has not advertised a place.
Relatives and acquaintances often know of free apprenticeship places.
An application list helps you keep track.
If you get no answer, you may politely ask after about two weeks.
For those under 18, the parents also sign the apprenticeship contract.
After an acceptance you politely withdraw from the other companies.

abschnitte.text: Many vacant apprenticeship places are listed on **apprenticeship exchanges** on the internet. A well-known one is **LENA**, the cantons' list of apprenticeship places, which you can find via berufsberatung.ch. Apprenticeship places are also advertised on **company websites**. If you really like a particular company, you can send a **speculative application**. Sometimes this leads to a chance even though no place was advertised.

Many apprenticeship places are given out through **contacts** before they are advertised publicly. That is why it is worth telling your parents, relatives, neighbours and acquaintances what you are looking for. Coaches at your sports club or teachers sometimes know a company too. This **network** can give valuable tips.

If you write lots of applications, you can quickly lose track. An **application list** shows when you applied where and how things stand. In it you note the date, the company, the contact person and the answer. If there is no answer after about **two weeks**, you may politely **follow up** by phone or email. This shows interest and commitment.

If it has worked out, an **apprenticeship contract** is signed. If the apprentice is not yet of age, the parents or the **legal guardian** also sign. After that the canton approves the contract. Once you have accepted a place, you **politely withdraw** all your other open applications. This way those companies can give the place to other young people.

Rejections are part of looking for an apprenticeship place and are normal. The important thing is to learn from them and keep going. The canton's **careers advice service** helps with the search and with improving your application. If you still have no apprenticeship place in the summer, you can attend a **bridging programme**, for example a tenth school year, and keep applying.

gewusst: In Switzerland most apprenticeships begin in August.
Many companies give out their apprenticeship places almost a year before the apprenticeship starts.

teile.einleitung: Bricklayers build walls on the building site from bricks and concrete. Without them there would be no houses, schools or bridges.
wichtigste: A bricklayer builds walls from stones and concrete.
Stones are joined with mortar so that the wall holds.
Concrete consists of cement, sand, gravel and water.
For straight walls the bricklayer needs a spirit level, a line and a plumb bob.
In Switzerland the apprenticeship as a bricklayer EFZ lasts three years.
The work usually takes place outdoors, in all weathers.

abschnitte.text: A **bricklayer** places stones on top of each other and so builds walls. He often uses **bricks** made of fired clay or **sand-lime bricks**. With the **trowel** he spreads **mortar** between the stones, a mixture of sand, binder and water. When the mortar hardens, the stones hold firmly together. The stones are laid staggered so that the wall is stable.

Many parts of a house are made of **concrete**, for example foundations, ceilings and cellar walls. Concrete consists of **cement**, sand, gravel and water. It is poured as a liquid into a mould, the **formwork**. Inside there are steel bars, the **reinforcement**. They make the concrete much stronger. After a few days the concrete is hard and the formwork can be removed.

A wall must stand **straight** and **vertical**. For this the bricklayer uses the **spirit level**, which shows whether something is horizontal or vertical. With a stretched **line** he keeps to the right line. The **plumb bob**, a weight on a string, points exactly downwards. He also reads **building plans** and measures where doors and windows will go.

In Switzerland the apprenticeship is called **bricklayer EFZ** and lasts three years. For a shorter training course there is the **construction assistant EBA**. Bricklayers usually work **outdoors**, in the heat in summer and in the cold in winter. They need strength, team spirit and a love of working with their hands. A helmet and safety boots are compulsory on the building site.

gewusst: The ancient Romans already knew a kind of concrete. The Pantheon in Rome has a huge dome made of Roman concrete that is almost 2000 years old.
A brick is just the right size to hold in one hand, so the bricklayer can use the trowel with the other hand.

teile.einleitung: Most young people in Switzerland do an apprenticeship after compulsory schooling. They learn in two places: at the company and at vocational school. That is why people speak of the dual education system.
wichtigste: “Dual” means two-track: you learn at the company and at vocational school.
The federal government, the cantons and professional organisations run vocational training together.
At federal level, SERI is responsible for vocational training.
A training company needs a training permit from the canton.
Germany and Austria also have a strong dual system.
The dual system helps keep youth unemployment low.

abschnitte.text: During an apprenticeship, apprentices work at the **training company** on several days a week. There they learn the practical side. On one or two days they attend **vocational school** and learn the theory. In addition there are **inter-company courses**, in which the basic skills of the job are practised. An apprenticeship with an EFZ lasts three or four years, and one with an EBA two years.

Vocational training is run jointly by **the federal government, the cantons and professional organisations**. This is called a **partnership**. At federal level the **State Secretariat for Education, Research and Innovation (SERI)** is responsible. It issues, for example, the training ordinances. The cantons put vocational training into practice and run the vocational schools. The **professional associations** decide what content a job needs, because they know the practical side best.

Not every company may train apprentices. It needs a **training permit** from the canton. The canton checks whether the company meets the necessary requirements, for example having a trained vocational trainer. For most training companies, training also pays off financially. According to SERI, the majority make a **net benefit**, because the apprentices' work is worth more than the costs.

Apprentices gain experience of the **job market** early on. That is why **youth unemployment** in Switzerland is low by international comparison. As well as Switzerland, **Germany and Austria** in particular have a strong tradition of dual apprenticeships. After the apprenticeship many paths are open, such as the vocational baccalaureate or higher vocational education.

gewusst: As well as the company and school, inter-company courses are seen as the third place of learning.
In Switzerland you can choose from around 250 different apprenticeship trades.

teile.einleitung: Holidays are paid days off that all employees in Switzerland have a right to. Apprentices and all young people up to their 20th birthday get a particularly large number of holidays. They are entitled to at least five weeks a year.
wichtigste: All employees in Switzerland have a right to paid holidays.
Adults get at least four weeks of holiday a year.
Young people up to their 20th birthday get at least five weeks.
This also applies to apprentices.
Holidays may not be paid out as money while the employment lasts.
At least two weeks of holiday should be taken in one block.
The rules are set out in the Code of Obligations.

abschnitte.text: Holidays are days when you do not have to work but still receive your **wages**. They are there for rest, so that you stay healthy and able to work well. The right to holidays is set out in the **Code of Obligations** (OR). A company may not agree to fewer holidays than the minimum.

Adult employees get at least four weeks of holiday a year. Young people up to the end of their 20th year get at least **five weeks**. Many companies and collective labour agreements voluntarily give more. The exact number is written in the apprenticeship contract.

Apprentices no longer have school holidays as before, but holidays like other employees. As a rule they should take their holidays when there are no lessons at the **vocational school**. Exactly when is agreed with the training company. The company takes their wishes into account, but has a say in the final decision.

At least two weeks of holiday must be granted **in one block**. During your holidays you may not work for money at another company if this gets in the way of your rest. If you fall ill during your holidays, the days of illness with a doctor's certificate usually do not count as holiday. Holidays may not simply be paid out while you are employed.

It is worth discussing your holiday wishes with the company early. You should note down how many **days of holiday** you have already taken. If anything is unclear, the cantonal vocational training offices or trade unions can help. Public holidays such as Christmas or 1 August do not count as days of holiday.

begriffe.erklaerung: An important Swiss law which, among other things, governs employment contracts.
People who are employed and receive wages.
A contract between employers and trade unions for a whole industry.
The number of days of holiday that you are entitled to.

gewusst: Young people get more holidays than many adults because they are still developing.
People with a part-time job also have a right to holidays, simply in proportion.

teile.einleitung: The SRG SSR is the largest media company in Switzerland and belongs to the public, not to a private owner. It includes SRF, RTS, RSI and RTR, which make radio, television and online content in all four national languages. It is paid for mainly by the media fee, which almost all households in Switzerland pay.
wichtigste: The SRG is Switzerland's public broadcaster.
It includes SRF, RTS, RSI and RTR as well as swissinfo.ch.
It makes programmes in German, French, Italian and Romansh.
The SRG was founded in 1931 and has its headquarters in Bern.
It is mainly funded by the media fee.
It has a legal mission known as public service.
Well-known programmes include, for example, the “Tagesschau” news and “Meteo”.

abschnitte.text: The **SRG SSR** is the Swiss Broadcasting Corporation, in German Schweizerische Radio- und Fernsehgesellschaft and in French Société suisse de radiodiffusion et télévision. It is organised as an association and so belongs not to a corporation but to its members and the public. It was founded in 1931, at that time only for radio. Its headquarters are in Bern.

The SRG is made up of several business units. **SRF** (Schweizer Radio und Fernsehen) broadcasts in German, RTS (Radio Télévision Suisse) in French and RSI (Radiotelevisione svizzera) in Italian. **RTR** (Radiotelevisiun Svizra Rumantscha) produces programmes in Romansh. In addition there is swissinfo.ch, which reports on Switzerland in ten languages.

The SRG runs many radio stations such as Radio SRF 1 or Radio SRF 3 and several television channels such as SRF 1 and SRF zwei. Well-known programmes are the “Tagesschau”, “10 vor 10” and, for children, “SRF Kids”. On the **Play Suisse** platform you can stream films and series from all parts of the country, often with subtitles. The SRG also broadcasts big sporting events such as ski races or matches of the Swiss national football team.

The SRG gets most of its money from the **media fee**, which is collected by the company Serafe. A household paid about 335 francs a year for it (as of 2025). The SRG earns a smaller part from advertising and sponsorship. Private local radio stations and regional television also receive a share of the fee.

The SRG has a legal mission known as **public service**. It is meant to provide all parts of the country and all language groups equally with information, education, culture and entertainment. In this way it helps the different regions of Switzerland to get to know and understand each other. The level of the fee and the size of the SRG are repeatedly debated and voted on in Switzerland.

begriffe.erklaerung: Services that are meant to benefit all people throughout the country.
A contribution that households and companies pay for radio and television.
Swiss Radio and Television, the German-speaking part of the SRG.
The fourth national language of Switzerland, spoken mainly in the canton of the Grisons.

gewusst: The Romansh unit RTR broadcasts for a language group of only about 60,000 people.
In March 2018 Swiss voters clearly rejected the “No Billag” initiative to abolish the fees.
The SRG is a member of the European Broadcasting Union, which organises the Eurovision Song Contest.

teile.einleitung: People who work also need rest. That is why the Code of Obligations (OR) sets out how many holidays employees in Switzerland must get at least and how they are taken.
wichtigste: Adults get at least four weeks of holiday per year of service.
Up to the end of their 20th year it is at least five weeks.
At least two weeks of holiday must be taken in one block.
The employer decides when, but takes the employee's wishes into account.
Holidays may not be paid out as money while the employment lasts.
With an hourly wage and four weeks of holiday, the holiday supplement is about 8.33 per cent.

abschnitte.text: Under **Art. 329a OR**, adults are entitled to at least **four weeks** of holiday per year of service. Anyone who is not yet 20 gets at least **five weeks**. Apprentices benefit from this above all. Employment contracts or **collective labour agreements** may provide for more holidays, but never fewer.

abschnitte.titel: When and for how long in one go
abschnitte.text: The **employer** decides when the holidays are taken. However, the employer must take the employees' wishes into account as far as the business allows. According to **Art. 329c OR**, at least two weeks of holiday must be taken in one block. Only then is real rest possible.

Holidays should really be taken. That is why **Art. 329d OR** forbids replacing them with money while the employment lasts. One exception is the **holiday supplement** for irregular hourly wages. With four weeks of holiday you work 48 of the 52 weeks, so the supplement is 4 divided by 48, which is about **8.33 per cent**.

If you are absent through no fault of your own, for example because of illness, you do not simply lose holidays. A reduction is only allowed once the absence lasts more than a month in total. For the second and every further full month, holidays may be reduced by **one twelfth**.

Young people up to the end of their 30th year can take up to one week of **youth leave** every year. It is meant for leading or supervising roles in youth work outside school, for example running a camp. The employer does not have to pay wages for this week.

gewusst: With five weeks of holiday, the holiday supplement for an hourly wage is about 10.64 per cent.
Youth leave is set out in Art. 329e OR and is important for many camp leaders.

teile.einleitung: In the Swiss education system, a path you have chosen is not fixed for ever. You can switch, catch up on something later or go further. This is called permeability.
wichtigste: Permeability means that you can switch between educational paths.
The guiding principle is: “No qualification without a next step”.
After an EBA you can often do an EFZ in a shortened apprenticeship.
With an EFZ, higher vocational education is open to you.
Adults can catch up on a vocational qualification.
Without a Matura, an entrance examination leads to ETH.

abschnitte.titel: No qualification without a next step
abschnitte.text: A **permeable education system** allows you to switch between different paths. For example, you can go from an apprenticeship to a university, or switch from upper secondary school (Gymnasium) to an apprenticeship. The guiding principle is **“No qualification without a next step”**. So every qualification should open the way to further training. This means a decision made at 15 is not final.

abschnitte.titel: From EBA to EFZ and beyond
abschnitte.text: Anyone who completes a two-year apprenticeship with an **EBA** can often gain an **EFZ** in the same occupational field in a **shortened apprenticeship**. The EFZ is the basis for **higher vocational education**. Anyone who has a few years of practical experience after the apprenticeship and passes the **professional examination** receives the **federal certificate**. After the advanced federal examination comes the **federal diploma**. Professional education colleges are also open to people with an EFZ.

Even with a **Matura** from a Gymnasium you can learn a trade. Some sectors offer shortened apprenticeships for this, for example in IT or as a commercial employee (KV). The other way round, there are paths to university without a Matura. **ETH**, for example, offers an **entrance examination** for people without a recognised Matura certificate. Anyone with a vocational baccalaureate can also go to a university after an additional examination, the **Passerelle**.

Adults without an apprenticeship can also catch up on a qualification. With the **vocational qualification for adults**, an EFZ or EBA is possible. Anyone with enough work experience, usually five years, can be admitted directly to the **qualification procedure**. In this way what you have learned at work counts too.

gewusst: In Switzerland you can get all the way to a university via an apprenticeship, the vocational baccalaureate and the Passerelle.
The shortened apprenticeship after the Matura is common in IT, for example.

teile.einleitung: Teachers teach children and young people new things. They explain reading, writing, maths and much more and help every child to make progress in learning.
wichtigste: A teacher teaches children new things at school.
She prepares lessons, teaches and marks work.
In Switzerland teachers are trained at universities of teacher education.
There are teachers for kindergarten, primary school, lower secondary school and other schools.
Teachers work closely with parents and other professionals.
In German-speaking Switzerland the Lehrplan 21 curriculum applies.

abschnitte.text: A **teacher** explains new things in a way that children understand. She sets tasks, answers questions and helps when someone is stuck. Besides teaching, she has a lot to do: she **prepares lessons**, looks for materials, **marks** tests and writes assessments. She also makes sure that everyone in the class feels comfortable.

Teachers work at different **levels**. In **kindergarten** the youngest children learn through play. In **primary school**, reading, writing and maths are added. In **lower secondary school**, teachers often teach only a few subjects. Later there are teachers at Gymnasiums and vocational schools. **Special needs teachers** are also part of the team; they support children who need extra help.

In Switzerland you learn the job at a **university of teacher education**, PH for short. For kindergarten and primary school, the bachelor's degree takes three years. For lower secondary school you need a **master's degree**. During your studies you already teach school classes yourself on placements. This way you learn theory and practice together.

A teacher does not work alone. She talks to the **parents**, for example at parents' meetings. She plans with other teachers and works with the head teacher, the school social workers or the school psychology service. What is learned at school is set out in German-speaking Switzerland in the **Lehrplan 21** curriculum.

gewusst: Johann Heinrich Pestalozzi from Zurich is seen as one of the best-known educators in the world. He wanted to develop the head, heart and hand.
During the eleven years of compulsory schooling in Switzerland, a child spends many thousands of hours in lessons.

teile.einleitung: Media literacy means being able to use media such as mobile phones, the internet, television and newspapers sensibly, critically and responsibly. It includes checking information, protecting yourself and creating your own content. In Switzerland you already learn this at school.
wichtigste: Media literacy means using media sensibly, critically and responsibly.
The term was coined by the educationalist Dieter Baacke.
In Lehrplan 21 you learn media literacy in the module Media and Computer Science.
The JAMES study regularly looks at how Swiss young people use media.
The federal platform Youth and Media promotes media literacy.
A comment gives a personal opinion, a news article informs.
Fixed phone-free times help against too much screen time.

abschnitte.text: **Media literacy** is the ability to deal with media wisely. The German educationalist **Dieter Baacke** coined the term (Medienkompetenz) in the 1970s. He distinguished several areas, including media criticism, knowledge about media, media use and media creation. So it is not just about operating devices, but also about understanding and taking part.

In **Lehrplan 21**, the curriculum used in German-speaking Switzerland, there is the module **Media and Computer Science** (Medien und Informatik). There pupils learn how media work, how to check information and how computers work. They also create texts, photos, videos or small programs themselves. The aim is for all children to be able to use digital media safely and confidently.

Since 2010 the **JAMES study** has looked every two years at how young people in Switzerland use media. It is carried out by the Zurich University of Applied Sciences (ZHAW) together with Swisscom. For younger children there is the MIKE study. The Confederation’s national platform **Youth and Media** (Jugend und Medien) offers information and tips for parents, teachers and young people.

Media-literate people ask themselves who is behind a piece of information. A website’s **legal notice** states who is responsible for the site. In a newspaper you should distinguish between a news article, which informs in a factual way, and a comment, which gives a personal opinion. You also need to be able to recognise advertising, even when it looks like a normal post.

Media literacy also includes keeping your own screen time under control. A good strategy is fixed phone-free times, for example at meals, while doing homework or before going to sleep. Many phones show how long you have used which app. It is also important to communicate in a friendly way and to respect other people’s privacy.

begriffe.erklaerung: Questioning and judging media and their content.
The shared curriculum of the cantons of German-speaking Switzerland.
A Swiss study about how young people use media.
Information about who is responsible for a website.

gewusst: The name JAMES stands for the German words for youth, activities, media, survey Switzerland.
According to the JAMES study, almost all young people in Switzerland have their own mobile phone.

teile.einleitung: A collective labour agreement, GAV for short, sets the working conditions for many employees at once. It is negotiated between trade unions and the employers' side and is an important part of the Swiss social partnership.
wichtigste: A GAV is concluded between employees' associations and employers or their associations.
It must be concluded in writing.
A GAV declared generally binding applies to all companies in an industry.
While it is in force, the peace obligation applies.
An individual contract may only differ from the GAV in favour of the employees.
The Peace Agreement of 1937 is seen as the foundation stone of the social partnership.

abschnitte.text: Under **Art. 356 OR**, **employees' associations**, that is trade unions, conclude a GAV with employers or **employers' associations**. It sets, for example, minimum wages, working hours, holidays or extra pay. According to **Art. 356c OR** it must be concluded in writing. This also applies to joining and terminating it.

Normally a GAV only applies to the members of the associations. With a **declaration of general applicability**, it is extended to all employers and employees in an industry, including non-members. If the GAV covers several cantons, the **Federal Council** decides; otherwise the canton does.

Under **Art. 357a OR**, the parties commit themselves to keeping **industrial peace** on the questions that are settled. Strikes and lockouts on these points are ruled out while the agreement is in force. On 19 July 1937, employers and trade unions in the metal and engineering industry concluded the **Peace Agreement**. They wanted to settle conflicts through negotiation rather than strikes.

Each person also has their own **individual employment contract**. If it differs from the GAV to the disadvantage of the employee, that agreement is void and the rule of the GAV applies. Differences in favour of the employee are allowed. This is called the **favourability principle**.

In the main construction industry, the **National Framework Agreement**, LMV for short, applies. It sets wages, working hours and other conditions. The LMV has been declared generally binding and is negotiated between the industry's employers' association and the trade unions.

gewusst: Many GAVs only apply for a few years and are then negotiated again.
Apprentices can also benefit from a GAV, for example through extra holidays.

teile.einleitung: Forestry workers work outdoors in the forest. They fell trees with a chainsaw, plant young trees and look after paths and protection forests.
wichtigste: Forestry workers almost always work outdoors in the forest, in all weathers.
They fell trees with a chainsaw and prepare the timber.
They plant young trees and look after the young forest.
The apprenticeship as a forestry worker EFZ lasts three years.
Safety is very important, so they wear a helmet and cut-resistant clothing.

abschnitte.text: One important task is **felling trees**. With the **chainsaw**, forestry workers first saw a notch into the trunk and then make the felling cut. This makes the tree fall in the planned direction. After that they remove the branches from the trunk and cut it into pieces. The wood is used for building, furniture or heating.

Forestry workers **plant young trees** and protect them from deer, which like to eat the buds. They remove shrubs that take the light away from the young trees. They keep **forest paths** in good repair and build fences or small barriers. This keeps the forest healthy.

In the mountains the forest protects villages and roads from **avalanches**, **rockfall** and landslides. This forest is called **protection forest**. Forestry workers make sure that it stays stable and that young trees keep growing back.

The apprenticeship as a **forestry worker EFZ** lasts three years. Because the work can be dangerous, apprentices learn a lot about safety. They wear a **helmet** with ear protection and a face guard as well as **cut-resistant trousers**. After the apprenticeship you can train further to become a forester.

gewusst: About a third of Switzerland's area is covered with forest.
Clear-cutting, which means felling all the trees on a large area, is forbidden in Switzerland.

teile.einleitung: The payslip shows how much you earn and what is deducted from it. If you can read it, you understand why less arrives in your account than is written in your employment contract.
wichtigste: The gross wage is the agreed wage before deductions.
After the social insurance contributions are deducted, what remains is the net wage, which is paid out.
According to Art. 323 OR, unless otherwise agreed, wages are paid at the end of the month.
A 13th month's salary is not required by law, only if it has been agreed.
For your tax return you receive a salary certificate every year.
Foreign employees without a C settlement permit usually pay withholding tax.
Since 2025, under federal law, the child allowance has been at least 215 francs a month.

abschnitte.text: Right at the top of the **payslip** is the **gross wage**. With an hourly wage you multiply the hours by the hourly rate: 160 hours at 28.50 francs gives 4560 francs. Then come the **deductions**. What is left is the **net wage**. Under **Art. 323 OR**, unless otherwise agreed, wages must be paid at the end of the month, and the employer provides a written statement.

Contributions to **social insurance** are deducted from the gross wage. The most important are the **AVS** (old-age and survivors' insurance), the **IV** (disability insurance) and the **EO** (income compensation scheme), which together came to 5.3 per cent for employees in 2025. On top of this there is **unemployment insurance**, above a certain wage the **pension fund**, and often insurance for accidents in your free time. For the AVS and unemployment insurance, the employer pays the same amount again.

Many employees receive a **13th month's salary**. However, the OR does not require it. It only applies if it has been agreed in the employment contract, in a **collective labour agreement** or through long-standing practice. If an annual salary is paid in 13 parts, you divide by 13: with 71,500 francs that is exactly 5500 francs a month.

Something can also be added on the payslip. Parents receive **family allowances**. Since 1 January 2025, the **child allowance** under federal law has been at least 215 francs per child per month, and this amount also applies in 2026. For children aged 16 and over who are in training there is the higher **training allowance**. The cantons may pay more.

Once a year, employees receive the **salary certificate**. It summarises all wage payments and deductions and is attached to the **tax return**. For foreign employees without a **C settlement permit**, the employer usually deducts the tax directly from the wages and pays it to the canton. This is called **withholding tax**.

gewusst: Employees pay AVS contributions from 1 January after their 17th birthday.
You should keep your payslips, because they help with questions about insurance and taxes.

teile.einleitung: The federal certificate (eidgenössischer Fachausweis) is a qualification in higher vocational education. It is awarded to people who have gained a few years of experience after their apprenticeship and passed the professional examination.
wichtigste: Anyone who passes the professional examination receives the federal certificate.
The professional examination is part of higher vocational education.
The examinations are run by professional organisations.
The examination regulations are approved by SERI.
The federal government refunds half of the eligible course costs, up to a maximum of 9500 francs.
In English the certificate is called the Federal Diploma of Higher Education.

abschnitte.text: The **federal certificate** is awarded after passing a **professional examination (BP)**. The professional examination is part of **higher vocational education**. It is aimed at experienced professionals who want to specialise or take on more responsibility. That is why most examination regulations require, as well as an upper secondary qualification, a few **years of work experience** in the field.

The examinations are developed and run by **professional organisations (OdA)**. These are professional and industry associations. They also draw up the **examination regulations**. In this way the qualifications are close to practice. The examination regulations are approved by the **State Secretariat for Education, Research and Innovation (SERI)**. This makes the qualifications recognised at federal level.

Many people prepare for the professional examination with courses. Since **2018** the federal government has supported candidates directly. It refunds **50 per cent** of the eligible course fees. Fees of up to 19,000 francs are counted, so the contribution is at most **9500 francs**. The money goes to the person, not to the school.

To receive the federal contribution, you must have **taken** the federal examination. Whether you pass does not matter, but you must sit it. You also need to be **resident in Switzerland** at the time of the examination. The invoices for the courses must be in your own name.

So that the qualification is also understood abroad, there is an official English name: **Federal Diploma of Higher Education**. The EFZ, by contrast, is called the **Federal VET Diploma**. After the federal certificate you can often take the **advanced federal examination** and gain a federal diploma.

gewusst: You receive the federal contribution to the courses even if you do not pass the examination.
The federal certificate is often the step before the federal diploma.

teile.einleitung: An employers' association is a group of companies that have joined together. It represents their interests in dealings with politicians, the authorities and trade unions.
wichtigste: Employers' associations represent the interests of companies.
The **Swiss Employers' Association** (SAV) was founded in 1908 and deals with employment and social policy.
**economiesuisse** was formed in 2000 from a merger and mainly represents economic policy concerns.
The **Swiss Trade Association** (sgv) mainly represents SMEs.
Industry associations such as **Swissmem** or the **Master Builders' Association** negotiate collective labour agreements with the trade unions.
**Joint committees** check whether a collective labour agreement is being kept.

abschnitte.text: In an **employers' association**, companies join together. Together they carry more weight than alone. The association represents their interests with politicians and the authorities, for example when new laws are being made. It also negotiates with the **trade unions**, which represent employees. Together, the two sides are called the **social partners**.

The **Swiss Employers' Association** (SAV) was founded in 1908. It represents employers mainly on questions of employment and social policy, for example AVS (old-age insurance) or unemployment insurance. **economiesuisse** was formed in 2000 from the merger of the Vorort and the Society for the Promotion of the Swiss Economy. It deals mainly with economic policy issues such as trade and taxes. The **Swiss Trade Association** (sgv) was founded in 1879 and mainly represents small and medium-sized enterprises, the **SMEs**.

As well as the umbrella organisations, there are associations for individual industries. **Swissmem** represents the mechanical, electrical and metal industries, the **MEM industries** for short. It negotiates the MEM collective labour agreement with the trade unions. The **Swiss Master Builders' Association** (SBV) represents the companies in the main construction trade. It negotiates the industry's collective labour agreement with the trade unions **Unia** and **Syna**.

A **collective labour agreement** (GAV) is a contract between employers or their associations and trade unions. It sets out, for example, minimum wages, working hours and holidays for a whole industry. Many collective labour agreements include a **peace obligation**: while the agreement applies, both sides give up strikes and similar measures. This cooperation is seen as a feature of the Swiss economy.

To make sure a collective labour agreement is kept, there are **joint committees**. “Joint” means that both social partners provide the same number of representatives. The committees check in companies whether, for example, minimum wages are being paid. If rules are broken, they can demand **inspection costs** or **contractual penalties**.

gewusst: The so-called Peace Agreement of 1937 in the engineering and metal industry is seen as the foundation stone of Swiss social partnership.
Compared with many other countries, there are only a few strikes in Switzerland. This is often explained by the close cooperation between the social partners.

teile.einleitung: Advertising is meant to make people aware of products, services or ideas and usually to get them to buy. We come across it everywhere: on posters, on television, in magazines, in free apps and from influencers. If you know how advertising works, you are less easily influenced by it.
wichtigste: Advertising usually wants you to buy something.
On the internet you can often recognise adverts by the word “Ad” or “Advertisement”.
In real life, products do not always look as great as they do in adverts.
A short advertising film before a video is called an ad or commercial.
Influencers sometimes show products because they are paid for it.
Many free games are funded by advertising.
If a game pushes you to buy something, ask your parents.

abschnitte.text: **Advertising** is a message that tries to win people over to a product, a brand or an idea. Companies pay for their adverts to appear on posters, on television, on the radio or on the internet. Political parties and charities also advertise to persuade people. Advertising is allowed, but it must be honest and must not deceive.

Advertising works with feelings, cheerful music, famous faces and catchy slogans. In commercials, toys are often shown bigger, more colourful and more exciting than they really are. For advertising photos, food is even made to look especially appetising by experts called **food stylists**. Another trick is time pressure, for example with “Today only!” or “Only 3 left!”.

On the internet you can often recognise advertising by the word **“Ad”** or “Sponsored”. Short advertising films called **ads** play before videos, and you close pop-up adverts with the little X. Many free games and apps earn their money from advertising and from purchases within the game, called in-app purchases. If a game pushes you to buy something, ask your parents first.

**Influencers** are people with lots of followers on social networks. Companies often pay them to show or praise products. Such posts should be clearly labelled as advertising, for example with “Ad” or “Paid partnership”. So not every recommendation is an honest opinion.

In Switzerland advertising must not lie or mislead; this is set out in the Unfair Competition Act. Anyone who thinks an advert is unfair can complain to the **Swiss Commission for Fairness in Advertising**. Strict restrictions apply to tobacco and alcohol, especially to protect children and young people. Children's programmes on Swiss television may not be interrupted by advertising.

begriffe.erklaerung: A short advertising film, for example before a video.
A paid advert in a newspaper or on the internet.
A person with lots of followers who influences others.
A purchase made inside an app or a game.
A name or sign by which you recognise a company's products.

gewusst: The first advertising posters appeared as early as the 19th century, when colour printing became possible.
Companies often pay a lot of money for their products to appear in films; this is called product placement.
Big companies spend billions on advertising every year.

teile.einleitung: An apprenticeship contract is a written contract between the apprentice and the training company. It contains everything important about the apprenticeship, for example its length, the wages and the holidays. The canton must approve the contract for it to be valid.
wichtigste: The apprenticeship contract is concluded between the apprentice and the training company.
It must be in writing.
For those under 18, the parents also sign.
The cantonal vocational training office approves the contract.
It sets out the length of the apprenticeship, wages, working hours, holidays and probationary period.
There is a probationary period at the start of the apprenticeship.

abschnitte.text: The **apprenticeship contract** is a special employment contract for the apprenticeship. It sets out the rights and duties of the apprentice and the company. It must be concluded in writing. If the apprentice is not yet 18, the parents also sign.

The training company sends the contract to the cantonal **vocational training office**. The office checks whether everything is in line with the law and approves it. The canton then registers the apprentice with the vocational school. It also **supervises** the apprenticeship and helps when there are problems.

The contract states the job, the start and the length of the apprenticeship. It also includes the wages for each year, the **working hours** and the number of weeks of holiday. The probationary period and insurance are also covered. There is a standard form for these contracts throughout Switzerland.

Every apprenticeship begins with a **probationary period** of one to three months. During this time both sides can check whether they suit each other. During the probationary period the contract can be terminated with seven days' notice. With the canton's consent it can be extended to a maximum of six months.

After the probationary period you cannot simply terminate an apprenticeship contract. It can only be ended by mutual agreement or for serious reasons. The canton must then be informed. If there is a dispute, the **apprenticeship supervisors** mediate between the apprentice and the company.

begriffe.erklaerung: A binding agreement between two or more people.
The first period of the apprenticeship, during which it is easier to part ways.
An office of the canton that oversees apprenticeships and helps with problems.
The firm where apprentices learn their job.

gewusst: If an apprenticeship contract is ended, the canton often helps to find a new apprenticeship place.
In Switzerland tens of thousands of new apprenticeship contracts are signed every year.

teile.einleitung: Kita is short for Kindertagesstätte, a day nursery. Small children are looked after there during the day while their parents work or are in training.
wichtigste: Kita is short for Kindertagesstätte, a day nursery.
The Kita mainly looks after children before they start kindergarten.
The children play, eat, rest and learn a lot.
Trained childcare workers look after the children.
In Switzerland the cantons or municipalities license and supervise the Kitas.

abschnitte.text: A **Kita** is a place where small children are **looked after** during the day. Many children start there as babies and stay until they go to **kindergarten**. Some are there every day, others only on a few days a week. The parents bring them in the morning and pick them up again in the evening.

At the Kita there is a fixed **daily routine**. The children play indoors and outdoors, sing, do crafts and listen to stories. Together they have their mid-morning snack, lunch and afternoon snack. After lunch the little ones often have an **afternoon nap**. Fixed routines give the children a sense of security.

Children learn a great deal at the Kita, mostly while **playing**. They learn to share with other children and to sort out arguments. They practise new words and explore their surroundings. Children who speak another language at home often already learn the **local language** at the Kita.

At the Kita, **childcare workers** and apprentices work. The manager often has higher training, for example as an **early childhood educator HF**. For a Kita to be allowed to open, it needs a **licence**. Depending on the canton, the canton or the municipality grants and checks this licence.

gewusst: Since 2003 the Confederation has supported the creation of new childcare places with a funding programme.
Many municipalities in Switzerland contribute to Kita costs so that more families can afford a place.

teile.einleitung: Train drivers drive trains. At the front, in the driver's cab, they make sure that passengers and goods reach their destination safely and on time.
wichtigste: The train driver sits in the driver's cab and drives the train.
He pays attention to signals, the timetable and the speed.
Technical safety systems stop the train if something is wrong.
Train drivers drive passenger trains or goods trains.
In Switzerland the railway is very important, and the trains are known for their punctuality.
The training is usually done as an adult after a first qualification.

abschnitte.text: The **driver's cab** is the train driver's workplace right at the front of the train. There are levers for accelerating and braking, screens and a radio. The train driver pays attention to **signals** beside the track or on the screen, keeps to the permitted **speed** and follows the **timetable**. At every station the train has to stop at exactly the right spot.

A train is very heavy and has a long **braking distance**. That is why technical systems help. The **train protection system** brakes the train automatically if it would pass a red signal or is going too fast. A **vigilance device** checks whether the driver is awake and paying attention. If he does not react, the train stops by itself.

Some train drivers drive **passenger trains**, from suburban trains to long-distance trains. Others drive **goods trains** carrying containers, cars or gravel. Because trains run early in the morning and late in the evening, train drivers often work **shifts**, including at weekends. Before setting off, they check the vehicle, for example the brakes.

Switzerland has a dense **railway network**, and people here travel by train a great deal. The largest railway company is the **SBB**, and there are many other railways such as the BLS or the Rhaetian Railway. Anyone who wants to become a train driver usually first completes an apprenticeship or other training and then special **training** with a railway company, with an examination set by the Confederation.

gewusst: At about 57 kilometres, the Gotthard Base Tunnel is the longest railway tunnel in the world. It opened in 2016.
A goods train can need more than a kilometre of braking distance before it comes to a stop.

teile.einleitung: The application file is the collection of all the documents you send to a company for an apprenticeship. It is like a business card and often decides the first impression.
wichtigste: An **application file** includes a covering letter, a CV, copies of school reports and other evidence.
**Taster placement reports** and aptitude test results are often included too.
Many companies want the application as a **PDF** by email or through an online portal.
You include school reports as **copies**, never the originals.
A good file is **complete, neat and free of mistakes**.
You adapt the file, especially the covering letter, to each company.
You ask **referees** for permission beforehand.

abschnitte.text: The application file includes the **covering letter**, the **CV** and copies of your **school reports**. Many companies also want to see **taster placement reports** and results of **aptitude tests**, for example from the Multicheck or Basic-Check. These documents show your performance and commitment. You always include school reports as copies, because documents are not always sent back.

A tidy file **free of mistakes** shows that you work carefully. Spelling mistakes, on the other hand, leave a bad impression. That is why it is best to have someone proofread your file. Your **email address** counts too: an address with your first name and surname looks serious. Nicknames or funny words do not belong in an application.

Today many training companies accept applications **digitally**, as a **PDF** by email or through an **online portal**. You should therefore have all your documents neatly scanned and ready. It is handy to collect everything in a single, well-named PDF file. The file should not be too big, so that it arrives safely.

A **referee** is a person who can give the company information about you. These are, for example, **teachers** or people in charge at a **taster placement company**. You give their name and their phone number or email address. It is important to ask them **for permission beforehand**. Then they are also prepared if someone calls.

Every company and every job has different **requirements**. That is why you adapt the file a little. Above all, the **covering letter** should be personal and show why you want to join this particular company. A letter that you send in the same form to all companies is quickly noticed. A tailored file shows real **interest**.

gewusst: Many companies only look at an application file briefly the first time they go through it. That is why a clear order is so important.
Templates and tips for application documents are available free from the careers advice service and on berufsberatung.ch.

teile.einleitung: In the past people spoke of the Kleinkinderzieher, or nursery nurse. Today the job in Switzerland is called childcare worker (Fachfrau or Fachmann Betreuung). These professionals look after small children in the Kita.
wichtigste: Nursery nurse (Kleinkinderzieher) is an older name.
Today the job is called childcare worker (Fachfrau or Fachmann Betreuung), FaBe for short.
The apprenticeship lasts three years and ends with the EFZ.
Childcare workers work, for example, in a Kita.
They play, sing, eat and do crafts with the children.

abschnitte.text: At the **Kita**, childcare workers look after small children. They **play**, sing, eat and do crafts with them. They comfort a child who is sad and help with getting dressed or washing hands. They watch how each child is developing and tell the parents about it.

The work is carefully planned. Childcare workers think up **activities** that suit the children's age. They arrange the rooms so that the children can play safely and discover a lot. They pay attention to healthy food, rest times and **safety**. Working together as a team is also important.

The apprenticeship as a **childcare worker EFZ** lasts three years. You choose a **specialism**, for example **children**, older people or people with disabilities. There is also a general training course that combines several areas. Lessons take place at vocational school.

After the apprenticeship you can train further, for example as an **early childhood educator HF** at a college of higher education. With this you can, for example, lead a group or a whole Kita. Patience, a love of children and a sense of responsibility are important for the job.

gewusst: Men also work in this job, but there are still only a few of them.
The abbreviation FaBe is widely used in Switzerland for this job.

teile.einleitung: A social network is a platform on the internet where people create a profile, connect with others and share photos, videos and messages. Well-known examples are Instagram, TikTok, Snapchat, YouTube, Facebook and X. For many young people social networks are part of everyday life; they are a lot of fun but also have risks.
wichtigste: Most big social networks require a minimum age of 13 in their rules.
Mark Zuckerberg founded Facebook in 2004.
Instagram and WhatsApp now belong to the company Meta.
The short-message service Twitter has been called X since 2023.
TikTok belongs to the Chinese company ByteDance.
With a hashtag such as #Switzerland you make posts on a topic easy to find.
With a private account only approved followers can see your posts.

abschnitte.text: On a **social network** you create a profile with your name, a picture and a few details. Then you can follow others, like posts, comment and post content yourself. An **algorithm** chooses which posts you see in your feed, depending on what you often look at. Most networks are free and make their money from advertising.

Facebook was founded in 2004 by **Mark Zuckerberg** and fellow students at Harvard University. Twitter followed in 2006; it has been called X since 2023, after the businessman Elon Musk bought it. Instagram started in 2010 and was taken over by Facebook in 2012, and WhatsApp was bought in 2014. In 2021 the Facebook group renamed itself **Meta**, and TikTok, from the Chinese company ByteDance, became popular worldwide from around 2018.

With a **hashtag**, a word with the # sign, posts on a topic can be found, for example #Switzerland or #SkiHoliday. Stories on Instagram usually disappear again after 24 hours. People who subscribe to someone else's content are called **followers**. With a private account only the followers you have approved can see your posts.

Most big networks such as Instagram, TikTok and Snapchat require a minimum age of **13** in their terms of use. In Europe WhatsApp requires a minimum age of 13. If you are younger, you should decide together with your parents whether and how to use a network. Many platforms have special settings for teen accounts, such as restricting messages from strangers.

Social networks help you stay in touch with friends, discover new things and be creative. At the same time they can eat up a lot of time, because they are deliberately designed to keep you there for a long time. Other risks are **cyberbullying**, false news and constantly comparing yourself with pictures that seem perfect. If you take breaks on purpose and set your account to private, you use networks more safely.

begriffe.erklaerung: Your own page on a network with your name and picture.
A person who has subscribed to an account's posts.
A keyword with the # sign that collects posts on a topic.
The list of posts that are shown to you.
A set of calculation rules that decides what you are shown.

gewusst: At the beginning Facebook was only meant for students at Harvard University.
The # sign is called the hash sign, and using it for hashtags was suggested on Twitter in 2007.
Many networks show advertising tailored exactly to the interests of their users.

teile.einleitung: The fire brigade comes when there is a fire. But it also helps with accidents, floods, storm damage and many other emergencies.
wichtigste: The fire brigade puts out fires and rescues people and animals.
It helps with road accidents, floods and storm damage.
In Switzerland you can reach the fire brigade on the emergency number 118.
Most fire brigades in Switzerland are volunteer (militia) fire brigades.
Large cities also have a professional fire brigade.

abschnitte.text: You can remember the fire brigade's tasks with four words: **rescue**, **extinguish**, **recover** and **protect**. First, people and animals are brought to safety. Then the fire is put out. After that the fire brigade clears up and protects the surroundings from further damage.

Many call-outs have nothing to do with fire at all. During **floods** the fire brigade pumps out cellars and builds barriers out of sandbags. After a **storm** it clears away fallen trees. At road accidents it frees trapped people and soaks up spilled oil.

In Switzerland most firefighters are **militia firefighters**. They have another job and turn out when the alarm goes. They train regularly in their municipality. Large cities such as Zurich, Basel, Bern or Geneva also have a **professional fire brigade** that is ready round the clock.

People who want to work for a professional fire brigade have usually completed an apprenticeship first, for example in a craft trade. After that comes training as a **professional firefighter**. Good fitness, team spirit and a cool head are important.

gewusst: In many Swiss municipalities there is a duty to serve in the fire brigade. People who do not serve often pay a substitute tax.
Many fire brigades have a youth fire brigade, where children and teenagers can already take part.

teile.einleitung: Data protection means that personal information about people is protected and may not simply be collected, passed on or misused. In Switzerland the Data Protection Act regulates how companies and authorities must handle personal data. Data protection helps to preserve your privacy, especially on the internet.
wichtigste: Personal data is any information about a particular person.
In Switzerland the Data Protection Act (FADP) regulates how personal data is handled.
The revised Data Protection Act has applied since September 2023.
At federal level, the FDPIC monitors compliance with data protection.
Health data is considered especially sensitive.
In the EU the General Data Protection Regulation, GDPR for short, applies.
Cookies are small text files in the browser.
If an app asks for permission to use the microphone, it wants to access it.

abschnitte.text: **Personal data** is any information relating to a particular person, for example name, address, date of birth, photos or the location of your mobile phone. Data protection is meant to prevent such data from being collected or passed on without good reason. Everyone should be able to decide for themselves what happens to their data. This is called **informational self-determination**. In the Federal Constitution, Article 13 protects privacy and protection against misuse of personal data.

Switzerland’s first **Data Protection Act** (DSG in German) came into force in 1993. Because the digital world has changed a great deal since then, it was completely revised. The revised act has applied since 1 September 2023. It now only protects the data of natural persons, that is, of people and not of companies. For breaches, the people responsible can be fined up to 250,000 francs.

At federal level, the **FDPIC** (EDÖB in German) watches over data protection; this is the Federal Data Protection and Information Commissioner. The commissioner supervises federal authorities and private companies and can open investigations. The cantons’ own data protection officers are responsible for cantonal authorities. Every person also has a **right of access**. So you can ask what data a company has stored about you.

Some data is so sensitive that it is especially protected. This includes **health data** as well as information about religion, political views or ethnic origin. Genetic data and biometric data such as a fingerprint are also included. Anyone processing such data must be especially careful. Often explicit consent is needed for this.

Many websites store **cookies**, small text files in the browser that remember settings, for example. Apps ask for **permissions**, for example for the microphone, camera or location. If you give a permission, you allow the app to access that function. That is why you should only allow what the app really needs. Good passwords and sharing photos and data sparingly give extra protection.

Since 2018 the **General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR)** has applied in the European Union. It is one of the strictest data protection laws in the world. When it was revised, the Swiss Data Protection Act was brought closely into line with the GDPR. The EU recognises that Switzerland has equivalent data protection. That is why data can be exchanged between Switzerland and the EU fairly easily.

begriffe.erklaerung: Any information that belongs to a particular person.
The Federal Data Protection and Information Commissioner, the federal data protection authority (EDÖB in German).
A small text file that a website stores in the browser.
Allowing an app to access a function such as the camera or microphone.
The right to find out what data is stored about you.

gewusst: Since 2023 Swiss law has required privacy-friendly default settings, known in English as “privacy by default”.
Every year the FDPIC publishes an activity report about its work.

teile.einleitung: A password is a secret word or a secret string of characters that you use to prove that an account really belongs to you. It works like a key to a front door, only on the internet. A good password protects your games, messages, photos and sometimes even money.
wichtigste: A password protects an account from other people.
You may only tell your password to your parents, nobody else.
A good password is long and not easy to guess.
Your own first name, your date of birth or “123456” are bad passwords.
It is best to use a different password for each account.
If someone knows your password, you change it straight away.
When you type it in, a password usually only appears as dots or stars.

abschnitte.text: A **password** is a secret code that only you know. Together with your **username**, it opens your account in a game, an app or on a website. The computer compares the password you type in with the one stored and only lets you in if the two match. So that nobody can read it over your shoulder, the screen usually only shows dots or stars while you type.

A strong password is long, ideally at least 12 characters. It mixes capital letters, small letters, numbers and special characters such as ! or #. A good trick is a **memory sentence**: “My dog Bello eats 2 sausages every single day!” becomes “MdBe2sesd!”. Even easier are several random words in a row, for example “Cloud-Bike-Cheese-Tower”.

Your first name, the name of your pet or your date of birth are bad passwords, because other people can guess them. “123456”, “password” or “qwertz” also appear every year on lists of the most common and least secure passwords. Criminals let computer programs try out millions of such words in a short time. That is why a short password can sometimes be cracked in seconds.

You only tell your password to your parents, not even to your best friend. Friendships can change, and then someone could write silly things in your name. A note with your password stuck to the screen is the worst place to keep it, because everyone can see it there. If someone finds out your password, you change it straight away and tell your parents.

You should use a different password for each account, because if one is stolen, the others stay safe. A **password manager** is a program that stores many passwords encrypted, so that you only have to remember one master password. Many services also offer **two-factor authentication**. Here you need a code as well as the password, which is sent to your phone, for example.

begriffe.erklaerung: The name you use to log in to an account.
Your personal area in an app, a game or on a website.
A program that keeps many passwords safe for you.
Double protection: password plus an extra code.
A person who wants to break into other people’s computers or accounts.

gewusst: For many years “123456” has been one of the most commonly used passwords worldwide.
Even soldiers in ancient Rome used secret passwords to tell friend from foe.
Many phones can also be unlocked with a fingerprint or face recognition instead of a password.

teile.einleitung: An online friendship is a friendship that you keep up over the internet, for example when gaming or in chats. Such friendships can be lovely, because you meet people with the same hobbies. But because you never know for sure who is behind a profile, it is important to be careful.
wichtigste: You may have friends online too, but carefully.
You never know for sure who is behind a profile on the internet.
If an online friend wants to meet, you tell your parents.
Secrets that an online contact asks you to keep, you may and should still tell.
If someone online asks for photos of you, you say no and tell someone.
If an online friend promises presents, you need to be careful.
You may block people who bother you.

abschnitte.text: Many children and young people get to know new people online, for example in games, chats or fan groups. That can be fun, because you meet people with the same interests. But real friends are usually people you also know in real life. With people you meet online, you need to pay special attention.

On the internet you never know for sure who is behind a **profile**. An account with a picture of a child may in fact belong to an adult. Some adults deliberately pretend to be children in order to win trust. This deliberate winning of trust with bad intentions is called **cybergrooming**.

You need to be careful if someone says: “This stays our secret”. Good friends do not ask you to keep secrets from your parents, so you tell them anyway. Someone who promises presents such as game currency or vouchers often wants something in return. If someone asks for photos of you, you say no and tell an adult.

If an online friend wants to meet, you tell your parents first. A meeting should only take place with an adult going along and in a public place.
